articles.title: Russell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’
articles.summary:
Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand says couple previously split up over his promiscuity

Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his…

blocks.text: Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his promiscuity but that he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.
Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand, 39, said they fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian found monogamy difficult.
She said: “I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people.”
Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a navy pinstripe suit and brooch on her left lapel, Laura entered the witness box at Southwark crown court on Wednesday.
Laura told the court she met Brand at the Edinburgh festival in 2006 after his show Shame, which was “very, very, very funny”, “extremely entertaining” and sexually explicit.

She said they met in the foyer of the Assembly Rooms, where Brand complimented her friend, who had a boyfriend. Laura recalled: “And he said to me: ‘But tell me you don’t have a boyfriend,’ and I said: ‘No, I don’t.’”

Laura recalled that Brand contacted her the next and they had oral sex. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked: “Did he want to have penetrative sex?” to which Laura replied: “I didn’t want to, but I don’t remember it even being a topic. I didn’t intend to and I don’t remember him asking.”

They began dating in September 2006 and Brand “absolutely” respected her wishes sexually, Laura said. Describing his treatment of her, she said: “Very caring, totally at my pace. I was not experienced, I had only had one partner before Russell and I felt entirely cared for, and looked after by Russell.”

But the court heard their relationship broke down over his cheating. Winter asked: “Did you become aware shortly thereafter that he was promiscuous and engaging in sexually activity with others?” Laura replied: “I was aware when I met him that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of that year that he was engaging with other women, yes.”

Laura said the couple split up in February 2007 because of his infidelity. “I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. We talked about it. I did find that difficult,” she said.

Laura said she was “heartbroken” after the breakup but that the pair resumed contact as friends in summer 2007. She said she became friendly again with Brand when his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry ended, and that they rekindled their romance in 2015, married two years later, and they now have three children together.

When asked if she was aware of Brand’s promiscuity during their time apart, Laura said: “I was very aware of it and I would read about regularly in the papers and he also told me, we talked about it.”
But both the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, and the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, objected when Winter asked Laura what her view was “as to the truth” of the criminal allegations her husband faces.
“She’s not here as an expert witness,” the judge said.
Winter then asked Laura to describe Brand, to which Laura replied: “Russell, my husband, is caring, he’s kind, he’s a wonderful father to our children, he’s an amazingly attentive husband.
“He’s got an eye for detail I’ve never known before. The way he treats me is to really know me, I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”
She continued: “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage. It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest.”

In cross-examination Karmy-Jones noted that Laura had been present throughout most of the trial and had taken notes. She also challenged Laura about how much contact she had had with Brand after their break up in 2007.
Laura said she had spoken to Brand after his marriage to Perry ended. “He called me after his marriage and gifted me meditation for me and my boyfriend at the time,” she said.

Brand nodded and smiled as Laura insisted that while they had not had a sexual relationship in the years before they got back together in 2015, they had spent time together by going to the theatre and watching box sets.

The prosecutor said that in 2017, shortly after the couple had their first child, Brand was a guest on the US talkshow, The Wendy Williams Show. She said the comedian had said of his relationship with Laura: “When we went out with each other we loved each other very much but I was in a phase where I thought the world was an amusement park made out of orgasms.”
Laura replied: “I’m not denying he said that. I probably didn’t watch it.”

Earlier, statements from two of Brand’s ex-girlfriends were read to the court, as they gave good accounts of his character. They also said he had cheated on them and they had supported him financially.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Alaska governor orders investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign
articles.summary:
Republican Mike Dunleavy plans search after Peltola accused of recruiting Dan Sullivan to confuse voters

The Republican governor of

blocks.text: The Republican governor of Alaska announced plans to launch a criminal investigation after a report accused the campaign of Democratic senate candidate Mary Peltola of trying to confuse voters by recruiting a candidate with the same name as her opponent.

Governor Mike Dunleavy wrote on social media that he was “directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted”.

It came after the New York Times published a damning report in which one of Peltola’s former staffers said that the Democrat’s campaign recruited people named Dan Sullivan to run for office against the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, to deliberately confuse voters.

Donald Trump also called for Peltola to be “removed from the Ballot and prosecuted” after the report. The US president previously condemned the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan and accused Democrats of putting an “imposter” on the ballot.

Peltola’s campaign had denied involvement in encouraging or soliciting Dan J Sullivan, a former educator with no political experience, to run against Dan S Sullivan, according to an Anchorage Daily News report from May.

But Duleavy said the report “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections” and that “Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support.”

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable,” Dunleavy wrote.
The New York Times report relied on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, as well as several other people who participated in or were told about the plan.
after newsletter promotion

Text messages and documents seen by the New York Times also shed light on the plan that Peltola’s campaign staff and senior aides in the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) hatched to encourage other people named Dan Sullivan to run.

articles.title: US economy grows faster than expected in report out just ahead of elections
articles.summary:
Growth is in sharp contrast to ​households’ assessment, reflected in ‌Trump’s record-low approval ratings

The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as resilient consumer…

blocks.text: The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven ⁠business investment more than ⁠offset the impact ​of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.

Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.
Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.

The strength in growth is in stark contrast to ​households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The report was published less than a week before Tuesday’s midterm ‌elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. The US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.

Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”

Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the ​strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.

Consumer spending, ​which accounts for more ​than two-thirds of the economy, increased at ​a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in ​the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate ​hiring are helping ​to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.

But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipated a slowdown in consumer spending.

articles.title: BMO, CIBC, RBC, TD Bank block personal AI agents, citing safety and security
articles.summary: Some of Canada's biggest banks say they will block AI agents like Meta’'s popular Muse assistant from directly accessing accounts and other information of their clients.

image.caption: Some of Canada's biggest banks say they will block or limit AI agents from directly accessing their clients' online bank accounts. (Dillon Hodgin/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New
Some of Canada's biggest banks say they will block AI agents like Meta’'s popular Muse assistant from directly accessing accounts and other information of their clients.
The move follows public warnings from the CEOs of RBC and BMO
Some of Canada's biggest banks say they will block AI agents like Meta's popular Muse assistant from directly accessing their clients' online bank accounts and other information.
Royal Bank, TD Bank, CIBC and Bank of Montreal each say the decision is aimed at protecting sensitive information.

Canada's big banks have invested billions in artificial intelligence in recent years, deploying the technology to save time on internal tasks like processing mortgage applications. However, the CEOs of RBC and BMO have recently warned that third-party artificial intelligence agents are not to be trusted with personal banking information.

With a client's authorization, AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's ChatGPT can connect to bank accounts and credit cards to monitor balances and transaction histories, as well as share tips on spending habits. Making purchases typically requires human approval.

Last week, Axios reported that major U.S. banks — including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo — have detected unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, and in some cases taking actions that appear to be independent of user instructions.
Anthropic files for potentially biggest IPO ever

CBC News asked Canada's top banks on Monday if they are seeing similar activity. Those that responded initially deferred to the Canadian Bankers Association, which does not comment on the operations of its individual members as a matter of practice.

In an email to CBC News on Wednesday, RBC spokesperson Jeff Lanthier said Canada's largest bank by assets carefully weighed the risk of third-party personal AI agents in its decision to block these applications from its online banking platforms.

items: Canada's big banks embrace AI as workers face job uncertainty
46% of Canadian CEOs eyeing AI-driven growth with smaller staff, poll shows

blocks.text: "We understand that this may be disappointing for the small portion of our clients who use these tools, and we make this decision with the safety and security of our clients and systems at the forefront," he wrote.
TD spokesperson Ada Lovelace Rampersaud says her bank will also block all third-party personal AI agents from direct access to banking information where authentication is required.

"Our focus is on helping build a future where trusted AI agents can create meaningful value for clients while protecting their privacy, security and control over their financial information," she wrote in an email on Wednesday.
"Clients should never share their TD log-in credentials, passwords, PINs or one-time passcodes with an AI agent or anyone else."
Likewise, CIBC spokesperson Deborah Rowe says her bank does not "support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts."

"We are following developments in personal AI agents closely as these technologies evolve," she wrote in an email. "Protecting clients, their accounts and their personal information is our priority, while we support innovation through secure, appropriately designed channels."
Scotiabank said it will limit third-party AI agents from its banking platforms while it monitors concerns.
RBC CEO says AI agents must earn trust
On Wednesday, RBC CEO Dave McKay reflected on how AI could reshape the banking industry in a LinkedIn post.
"As these systems become more autonomous, the stakes go up when something goes wrong — from fraud and consumer harm to risks that could ripple more broadly through the financial system," he wrote.
"If AI is going to move beyond the frontier and into the broader economy, trust will matter as much as capability."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly Tai Po fire, pledges reform
articles.summary: John Lee also announces the resignation of Hong Kong's Housing Secretary Winnie Ho — the first official to resign over the inferno

blocks.text: APOLOGY. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee and other officials bow in apology during a press conference to announce the findings of an investigation into the 2025 fatal fire in Tai Po, Hong Kong, on October 29, 2026.
Tyrone Siu/Reuters
John Lee also announces the resignation of Hong Kong's Housing Secretary Winnie Ho — the first official to resign over the inferno

items: Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized for a deadly fire that killed 168 people, and released a report holding four government departments partially responsible for safety failures.
The report detailed governance issues, including bid rigging, and called for extensive reforms in the building industry.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

HONG KONG – Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized on Thursday, October 29, for the deadly blaze that killed 168 people in the city last November, as he released an independent report that held four government departments partially responsible for a fire that erupted after more than a year of safety complaints.

Lee promised swift but extensive reforms to the city’s building industry and regulatory system. The more than 1,000-page report by the judge-led panel detailed governance and supervisory failings, including widespread bid rigging.
“The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun,” the report stated.
“The Committee finds that no Government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum.”

The blaze ripped through seven 31-story tower blocks at the Wang Fuk Court residential complex, which was undergoing renovation work in the northern Tai Po district and shrouded in dust netting and scaffolding.
Residents had repeatedly raised safety concerns over the work for more than a year before the fire, which the report said was most likely started by a “glowing source…likely a cigarette.”
It was the deadliest in the city since 1948. Thousands of residents were displaced after their homes became uninhabitable.
“As chief executive and head of the government, I am deeply saddened,” Lee said before bowing with seven other officials in a rare show of official contrition.
“On behalf of the SAR government, I offer my apologies to the victims and the public at large.”
Lee also announced the resignation of Hong Kong’s Housing Secretary Winnie Ho — the first official to resign over the inferno.
Wang Fuk residents and other critics have in recent months expressed anger at a perceived lack of government accountability.
The Hong Kong government has set up an independent team to investigate which officials should be held accountable and to outline disciplinary actions.

Lee, whose five-year term ends next June, did not directly respond to press questions over whether he would seek another term, saying “implementing the reforms is the goal” rather than personal matters.

Lee said Hong Kong’s Chief Secretary Eric Chan will now head a steering committee to oversee reforms advocated in the report, which will include laws to criminalise bid rigging across the construction industry with fines of up to HK$10 million and 10 years’ imprisonment.
The committee report said contractor Prestige Construction & Engineering Co Ltd and project consultant Will Power Architects Co Ltd should bear primary responsibility.

At least 25 criminal charges related to the Wang Fuk Court fire have been made against Prestige, Will Power and seven individuals, including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering and tax evasion.
But the report also went further, outlining widespread unlawful and dubious construction practices as a “corrupt eco-system.”
The rigging of bids in the industry involved many different parties, some linked to triad organized crime gangs, it said.

The committee held 30 hearings this year with 80 witnesses, including residents, property management and renovation personnel, engineering and fire experts, government officials and regulators. It evaluated more than one million files and submissions as it investigated the cause of the fire and reviewed oversight of building renovations.

Before the report’s release, critics had said the committee lacked the statutory powers of a full public inquiry, which could potentially limit its ability to establish the full facts and accountability.

Some groups in the Asian business hub have called for more transparency and accountability, amid warnings from authorities that any attempts to politicise the disaster would be severely punished. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback
articles.summary:
As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming

CDs appear to be

blocks.text: CDs appear to be having a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%.
With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.
‘I have well over 10,000 CDs’

blocks.caption: Andrew Wales says his wife is very considerate about his CD collection.
More of Wales’s CD collection.

blocks.text: Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.

“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”

Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”
That said, Wales also owns “about 2,000 LPs”, “a few hundred cassettes” and an increasing number of Blu-rays. “I’m not always wedded to a single format.”
‘After having a baby, our records were too bulky and inconvenient’

blocks.caption: Gabriela Crowley with her daughter and her CD player.

blocks.text: Unlike Wales, Gabriela Crowley, 32, from San Jose, California, started listening to CDs only over the last year. “Growing up, my parents had a tonne of them,” she says. “My dad played them in the car and everywhere. And then he got an iPod. By the time I was like 18, everything had started to shift away from physical media.”

Her return to physical records started with the vinyl trend a few years ago. “I met my husband, who also had a large record collection, and we enjoyed that hobby together for a while. But after having a baby, we found we really weren’t listening to our records much any more – they were too bulky and inconvenient. My father-in-law gave us one of his old CD players and now we use that every day.”

A CD collection helps with the “paradox of choice” that streaming brings, she says. “Instead of being paralysed by the endless options, you become more intimately familiar with what you have. I find it a much more satisfying way to engage with music. Plus, no autoplay or AI-generated playlists are being forced on me.”
‘I buy CDs directly from the bands’

blocks.caption: Neil Cumming has several hundred CDs from classical to folk, rock and blues.

blocks.text: “I bought my first CD in 1988 and have been collecting ever since,” says Neil Cumming, 53, from Gloucester. “I have several hundred of them. Everything from classical, folk, rock, blues …”

Cumming buys CDs mostly to support musicians. “I like a lot of small indie and folk bands, who are not making a lot of money. I buy CDs directly from them when I can, which means they get a bigger share of my money than they would if I streamed their music.

“And it means I own the CD for ever,” he says. “Streaming means you are basically renting the music, and it can disappear from the streaming sites. I enjoy the ritual of selecting a CD and putting it in the machine – it is a nicer experience than just pressing play on an app.”

Not that he’s anti-streaming. “It’s quite good for trying music before you buy CDs or finding new acts. But in the evening, with a mug of tea or a glass of whisky, I find the experience of a CD more satisfying.”

blocks.caption: Asha Varadharajan says the patience required in listening to a whole CD makes songs memorable.

blocks.text: “I am drawn to the narrative and aesthetic arc of an album,” says Asha Varadharajan, 65, from Toronto. “It’s the antithesis of scrolling. I’ve never been a fan of music as white noise in the background, unless I’m boogying while vacuuming.”
Varadharajan has owned her CD player since 1999, “which allows me to listen to five CDs at a time in any order I choose, building my own narrative arc as I listen.

“I’m grateful to friends who introduced me to artists I may never have listened to,” she says. “The patience and persistence required in listening to a CD makes songs memorable. Streaming makes music ephemeral. I think algorithms make everything predictable, but everybody’s taste is kind of random.”
It helps that CDs are hard to damage, she says. “I’m a klutz and was terrified of scratching albums as a child because I never could place the needle accurately without my hand shaking.”

blocks.caption: Varadharajan’s CD player allows her to listen to five CDs at a time ‘in any order I choose’.

blocks.text: ‘They give me something tactile and tangible’

Ed, 63, from London, bought his first CDs in 1986 – “Genesis, Invisible Touch, and Level 42, World Machine, if you must know” – and has “never stopped”, he says. “But my interest in the format has waxed and waned.

“When they first came out, CDs were very much positioned as: they’ll last for ever, you can drill holes in them, you can put jam on them and they still play. But I got put off CDs because they sounded too bright and shiny compared to vinyl.”

But over the past two years, Ed has bought more CDs owing to their “almost throwaway prices against the excessive costs of vinyl”. Having music on CD “gives me something tactile and tangible”, Ed says. “A good digital source is now every bit as engaging as a good record player.”

articles.title: Two Colorado college students found dead after going missing during hike
articles.summary:
Kaden Matsuda and Jackson Donlon were on a trip in Rocky Mountains last weekend when heavy snowstorm hit

Two Colorado college…

blocks.text: Two Colorado college students have been found dead after going missing during a hiking trip in the Rocky Mountains last weekend when a heavy snowstorm hit, authorities said.

The bodies of Kaden Matsuda, 19, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Jackson Donlon, 20, of New York, were found on Wednesday afternoon in a basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles (160km) south-east of Aspen, the Chaffee county sheriff’s office said in a statement posted on social media.

The pair left Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus on Friday, telling family and friends they planned to hike up Ice Mountain, a nearly 14,000ft (4,270-meter) peak near West Apostle Mountain that requires technical climbing, the sheriff’s office said. They were expected back by Sunday, but college staff reported them missing on Monday morning.

The sheriff’s office said the causes of their deaths were under investigation, but foul play was not suspected. Authorities said they would not offer theories on what may have happened until autopsies are completed.

“Our heart aches for Kaden and Jackson’s family and friends,” Chaffee county’s sheriff, Andy Rohrich, said in the statement on Wednesday night. “We are very proud of our team’s efforts to find them before this weekend’s coming storm. Although this is a gut punch, our prayers were answered that we would find Kaden and Jackson, allowing some closure for the family.”
About 60 search and rescue volunteers, aided by helicopters, drones and dogs, searched for the two men.

The helicopter crew on Tuesday discovered a tent collapsed under the snow with their sleeping bags, a stove and clothing near a lake north-west of Ice Mountain, but the students were nowhere to be found.
Based on the tent’s location, officials said they were aiming for the 13,597ft West Apostle Mountain.
Friends and family described both men as experienced hikers and climbers.

The sheriff’s office said their climbing equipment was not in their dorms, tent or vehicle, suggesting they left their tent prepared for a technical climb. Trash inside the tent indicated they had eaten before starting their hike, officials said.
Matsuda was studying to become a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was studying to become a mountain guide, Rohrich said.
Authorities had been concerned that aerial searches could be limited later this week because of poor weather that is expected to begin on Friday.

articles.title: Survey period didn't cover hearings on alleged unexplained wealth, says prosecutor
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel has no reason to be demoralized amid the latest Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey showing that 35% of Filipinos are dissatisfied with the prosecution of the impeachment…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 8:56pm

The House prosecution panel has no reason to be demoralized amid the latest Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey showing that 35% of Filipinos are dissatisfied with the prosecution of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte, House prosecution panel spokesperson Zia Adiong of Lanao del Sur said Thursday.

Adiong said that the said poll was conducted last Septmber 21 to 27, a period that did not cover the prosecution’s presentation of evidence of the Vice President’s financial records which seeks to prove Article 2 or the Vice President’s alleged accumulation of unexplained wealth due to undeclared assets and non-divestment in businesses as mandated by the Constitution.

“The survey is not supposed to demoralize the prosecution because our track is based on a constitutional premise: Accountability. We all saw how the trial went. The Vice President was given due process to explain herself,” Adiong said in a press conference.

“The prosecution’s focus is really to hold the Vice President to account based on constitutional duty. The survey is not for us and may speak of different things. It cannot be automatically translated into the prosecution doing not the right thing,” he added.

The impeachment case against the Vice President rests only on one: Article 2 which alleges unexplained wealth due to non-declaration of assets in the SALN and non-divestment of businesses despite Constitutional prohibition.

The House prosecution panel dropped three charges of impeachment including: Article 1 on confidential fund, Article 3 on bribery and Article 4 on grave threat to President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. and his family after lawyer and certified public accountant Alex Cabrera testified that the Vice President and her husband said recorded P817 million unexplained wealth at the minimum and P1.5 billion at the maximum.

Cabrera made the conclusion after reviewing the financial records of the Vice President and her husband which include: SALNs, bank transaction and bank deposit records, insurance payment records, income tax returns and corporate records of the busines interests of the Duterte-Carpio couple.
“What drives us to move forward is the constitutional duty of the prosecution to hold the Vice President to account,” Adiong said.
Likewise, Adiong said the same survey showing that 78% of respondents believes it is important for the Vice President to testify personally to address the allegations against her.
“There is a high percentage of the public who wants the Vice President to explain, and that speaks a lot on the a public clamor for an explanation directly from the Vice President,” Adiong said.
“That speaks about their belief that an irregularity happened and that is the most important thing that we need to focus on,” he added. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: ​Pragmatic or pointless? Europe’s rift over whether to pick up the phone to Putin
articles.summary:
With no single European representative negotiating directly with Moscow, some leaders are establishing their own channels – with messy results

The Nordic countries rarely fall out in public…

blocks.text: The Nordic countries rarely fall out in public over foreign policy, least of all over Russia.
But a 90-minute phone call this week to Vladimir Putin by the leaders of Finland and Norway drew an unusual rebuke from their Danish and Swedish neighbours.

On Tuesday, Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, spoke with Putin, in a rare high-level conversation between the Russian leader and Ukraine’s European allies. The two Nordic leaders stressed that the call had been conducted on Ukraine’s behalf and that allies had been informed in advance.
Their neighbours were not convinced.

“I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” said Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, who complained that the call had not been coordinated with Copenhagen. “I honestly don’t know what they think they can achieve by this.”
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, also criticised the initiative, saying he had not been informed beforehand.

The friction offered a glimpse of the divisions threatening to complicate Europe’s attempts to establish its own channel to Moscow, as governments struggle to agree not only on whether to engage Putin but also on who should speak on their behalf.

“Instead of looking like a firmly united, homogeneous group, we see a rift,” said Arkady Moshes, director of the Russia programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. “By the standards of the Nordic world, it’s pretty serious.”

blocks.caption: Støre (centre) and Stubb (right) with Ukraine’s leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, earlier this month. Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix/AP

blocks.text: Since the summer, European leaders have been discussing, without much progress, whether to appoint a representative to negotiate directly with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine. The debate has grown more urgent as Donald Trump has moved closer to Moscow in recent weeks at Ukraine’s expense.

A new round of peace talks is expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month, leaving European governments anxious about being sidelined in negotiations that could shape the continent’s security for decades.

“There is an agreement overall that we need to talk to Putin, but the outreach is starting to feel like a free-for-all,” said a senior European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. “Too many leaders believe they can be the one to get Putin to negotiate.”
Mixed messages

This year, British, French and German ambassadors have held talks with Russian officials, Emmanuel Macron’s senior diplomatic adviser has travelled to Moscow, and the office of the European Council president, António Costa, has pursued its own engagement with the Kremlin.

It is a far cry from the diplomatic isolation imposed on Putin after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when most European leaders largely shunned direct contact with the Kremlin. Stubb himself said during his 2024 presidential campaign that he would not pick up the phone if Putin called.

Analysts this week blamed some of the fallout from the Stubb/Støre call on mixed messages about what it was actually for. Initially framed as an effort to convey Ukrainian messages to Putin, the call appeared to have broader aims.

Støre later defended Norway’s decision to engage directly with Putin, citing the need to manage shared fish stocks in the Barents Sea and maintain security along the countries’ common border. Stubb, meanwhile, said the conversation was also intended to prevent misunderstandings between Russia and its Nordic neighbours.

“Stubb and Støre can’t seem to get their message straight on whether this was about Ukraine or also about their own security concerns,” said Joel Linnainmäki, a former Finnish diplomat and analyst in Helsinki.
“If it looks messy, it probably is.”

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia last month. As the Ukraine war grinds on, the diplomatic isolation imposed on Russia is starting to crumble. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The confusion reflects a wider disagreement across Europe over how to approach Putin, even as governments remain broadly united in their support for Ukraine.

“On substance there is actually quite a good level of unity in Europe, but then there are different views on how to approach Russia, when is the right time to reopen dialogue at the highest level and who should be doing it,” said Kristi Raik, director of ICDS, a leading Estonian thinktank.

France has long advocated keeping a channel to Putin open, while Germany and Britain have been more cautious. The Baltic states and Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, fear that renewed high-level engagement could ease pressure on Moscow without securing concessions.
The question of who should lead any European outreach has proved contentious.

Xavier Bettel, Luxembourg’s foreign minister and one of the few European leaders to have maintained telephone contact with Putin after the full-scale invasion, recalled facing criticism from European colleagues for taking the initiative.

“Some colleagues told me: who is the Luxembourgish prime minister to speak to the president of Russia and the president of Ukraine? You are such a small country,” he said at a conference in Prague in May.
“That’s also a problem of the state of mind of some countries who think only France, Germany or the USA can lead discussions.”
after newsletter promotion
No single EU representative
For now, no single figure has a clear mandate to negotiate on behalf of the EU’s 27 member states.

In theory, the task of speaking to Moscow could fall to Kallas. But she lacks the independent authority to negotiate on behalf of the bloc without a mandate from its member states, and there has been growing frustration in European capitals over the EU’s diplomatic service, which she leads.

Kallas, a former Estonian prime minister and one of the EU’s most vehement Kremlin critics, is also seen by many as an unlikely interlocutor for Putin. Moscow has placed her on a wanted list, while Russian officials have made clear they have little appetite for engaging with her.

blocks.caption: The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, is seen as an unlikely interlocutor. Photograph: Harry Nakos/AP

blocks.text: Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European parliament, has called on EU leaders to convene a summit and agree on a single representative to engage with Putin.
He said: “The EU must speak with one voice, and Ukraine must always be involved. If you take those two things into account, then I think it makes perfect sense for Europe to engage in talks.”
But he acknowledged that reaching a unanimous agreement would be difficult, with any proposed appointment potentially vulnerable to a veto by a single member state.
In the meantime, this week’s Nordic initiative could encourage more European politicians to establish their own channels to Moscow, said Linnainmäki.
“It’s inevitable that politicians around Europe will now raise the question: if the Finns and Norwegians are calling Putin, why should our country not do it?” he said.
‘Putin’s plan A’
Beyond the question of who should speak to Putin lies a more basic question: whether there is any point in Europe talking to him at all.
Raik warned that Putin might interpret Europe’s sudden interest in reopening dialogue as a sign that Ukraine and its allies were growing desperate, with Kyiv facing a difficult winter.

“My concern is that the way the Kremlin is reading this step now is that the Europeans are in trouble, the Ukrainians are in trouble,” she said. “Knowing how Putin looks at Europe, I think he’s always keen to try to use opportunities to create divisions, or at least appearances of division,.”
The Kremlin’s account of Tuesday’s conversation offered little indication of any change in Putin’s maximalist demands for ending the war.

blocks.caption: Moscow has appeared more open to European diplomatic efforts since US special envoy, Steve Witkoff, met Putin last week. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Reuters

blocks.text: According to the Financial Times, Putin spent part of the conversation lecturing the Nordic leaders on medieval Slavic history, repeating pseudo-historical arguments that have long been used to question Ukraine’s right to exist as an independent state.
Still, Moscow has appeared more willing to entertain European involvement in diplomacy since US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg last week.
Moshes suggested that Moscow was tiring of Trump’s unpredictability and looking to Europe as an alternative, calculating that the US midterms could leave the president politically weakened.
But Putin’s willingness to take the call should not be mistaken for a readiness to compromise, Moshes cautioned.
“It doesn’t mean we are moving anywhere towards a ceasefire, let alone peace, because it’s clear that Putin’s plan A is a military defeat of Ukraine.”
Shaun Walker contributed reporting

articles.title: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist
articles.summary: ‘Compliance managers’ to have discussions with authority’s wealthiest customers in attempt to raise tax revenues

blocks.text: The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought.

In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authority said it was allocating a customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage.
“Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.

It said the managers would offer voluntary discussions to each billionaire before they filed their taxes, to “help build a shared understanding of the customers’ UK tax affairs and make subsequent engagement more focused and proportionate”.

The authority also plans to start deploying new tech to monitor wealthy individuals – defined as those with income of more than £200,000 or assets over £2m in any of the last three years – involving “advanced analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify emerging risks earlier and target compliance activity where it will have greatest impact”.

It is part of wider efforts to tackle the wealthy tax gap, whereby rich people are failing to pay what they should if all of their assets were disclosed to the tax authority. The wealthy tax gap for 2024-25 was estimated to be worth £3.6bn, equivalent to 6% of the total tax gap across the UK’s entire tax-paying population.
The tax authority said its actions would contribute at least £500m towards a larger commitment to raise £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.
after newsletter promotion
HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.

Adam Craggs, the head of tax, investigations and financial crime at the law firm RPC, said anyone with more than £200,000 of annual income, or net assets above £2m, should now “reflect on how clearly they understand and can evidence their UK tax position and their interaction with HMRC”.

articles.title: Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown
articles.summary: The Volkswagen Group has filed its worst quarterly performance since the height of the "Dieselgate" scandal in 2015. Share prices climbed in response, however, perhaps because the bad news was so…

image.caption: The VW group has been selling roughly 10% fewer units worldwide, but at slightly higher average prices compared to last year [FILE: March 7, 2025]Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.
The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.
It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.
"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

blocks.caption: During his state visit to core auto market China this week, German Presidnet Frank-Walter Steinmeier went to the Volkswagen China LabImage: Frank Ossenbrink/IMAGO

blocks.text: What were the main takeaways from VW's Q3 figures?

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.
Here are some of the key Q3 figures:

items: An operating loss of €5.86 billion, compared to €1.3 billion in same quarter last year
It's the company's worst single quarterly loss since the height of the "Dieselgate" emissions scandal in 2015
Sales revenue dipped 6.3% year-on-year, to €75.3 billion
Deliveries to customers, unit sales, and unit production numbers all dipped by roughly 15% as the company starts to reduce production levels, trying to adjust to falling demand

blocks.text: And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:

items: Sales revenue of €233.4 billion was broadly comparable to 2025's figure of €238.7 billion
But vehicle unit sales, at 5.9 million, are 11% lower than 6.6 million last year — meaning the group is selling fewer cars, at higher prices
The company's order intake for new cars rose 4% year-on-year, and by 39% for battery electric vehicles (BEVs)
Operating profit lies at just €0.1 billion, compared with €5.4 billion a year ago
But VW said 'special items' amounting to €8.7 billion primarily explain this massive dip
Non-cash writedowns on Porsche assets worth €6.4 billion were the largest portion of this

blocks.text: Can Volkswagen stage an automotive comeback?
How did investors respond?

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.
Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.
By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.
Volkswagen crisis: Emden plant closure impacts whole region
What are VW's downsizing plans?

CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.
Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.
CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.
Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.
"That is not enough in the long term," he said.
As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.
This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.
Germany under pressure

blocks.text: Business
Rising cost pressures and tough regulatory scrutiny over the treatment of gig workers have spurred deals in the industry, with many smaller players being eaten up by competitors in recent years.

DoorDash said on Thursday it would buy Instacart in a deal valued at about $17 billion US, stepping up its push ‌into the fast-growing U.S. grocery delivery market as competition among app-based platforms intensifies.
DoorDash has offered Instacart shareholders $65 per share held, representing a premium of about 26 per cent to ​the stock's closing price on Oct. 22, ​before reports of deal talks first emerged.
Delivery companies are chasing growth by expanding into grocery and retail ​as the restaurant delivery business matures.
"Grocery is one ⁠of the hardest ⁠things to get right ‌online," said Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, adding that Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers.
Meal kit companies now starved for customers after COVID-era boom

Grocery deliveries are gaining traction as budget-conscious consumers embrace ⁠the convenience of online deliveries, especially when gas prices have hit new highs due to disruptions linked to the war in Iran.

Meanwhile, heightened ‌competition following a slowdown in orders from the pandemic peaks, along with rising cost pressures and tough regulatory scrutiny over the treatment of gig workers, has spurred a flurry of ​deals in the industry.

items: Pandemic expanded online grocery shopping and delivery, but experts say in-store customers will be back

articles.title: John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share prices
articles.summary: Treasury select committee asks FCA to investigate whether tax surcharge leak led to ‘improper release of inside information’

blocks.text: John Healey is facing pressure to clarify whether he permitted a market-sensitive budget leak before his statement, which moved bank share prices.

The chair of the influential Commons Treasury select committe, Meg Hillier, has written to the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority watchdog (FCA) to assess whether a story leaked to Bloomberg, and published more than an hour before the budget was revealed, led to an “improper release of inside information”.

Shortly before Healey left Downing Street to deliver his budget statement in the Commons at 12.30pm, the prices of shares in banks moved as Bloomberg had published a story at 10.45am noting the bank corporation tax surcharge would be lower than the 8% that lenders had feared, and the increase would only be temporary.

In a letter to James Bowler, the permanent secretary of the Treasury, and the chief executive of the FCA, Hillier wrote: “There were two elements to the Bloomberg story, namely that the bank surcharge would not reach 8% and that it would be temporary.

“HM Treasury’s Budget 2026 confirmed the following: ‘Bank Surcharge: Temporarily increase the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge rate from 3% to 6%, to fund breathing space measures for households, for 15 months from 1 January 2027’. The Bloomberg story quoted ‘people familiar with the matter’.
“This appears to have been more than idle speculation, and it had implications for relevant securities.”

Writing directly to the FCA, Hillier noted the body’s responsibility for “market cleanliness” and its implementation of “the UK’s market abuse regulation”, adding, “I would welcome your view on whether this event might be considered an improper release of inside information and your assessment of its impact on the market in relevant securities.”

Separately, she urged Bowler to confirm “that banks (or any representatives of them or their trade bodies) were not told of the changes in outline or with specifics before” the budget and “how many people had access to the information” related to the bank surcharge changes.

Healey confirmed the surcharge would rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 as he told MPs in the Commons: “I am looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families. And so banks will pay an extra 3% on the bank surcharge. This will be time-limited to pay for immediate support on energy bills, starting in January, ending 15 months later.”
Commons sources are concerned that bankers were able to make money out of the measures that were leaked to Bloomberg an hour and a half before the measures were confirmed.

The chancellor will be asked to explain this leak when he appears before the Commons Treasury select committee next month. But in the meantime, Hillier has urged the Treasury and the FCA to investigate what happened and to confirm that “banks were not told of the changes in outline or with specifics before the publication of the budget”.

articles.title: Humanitarian aid expected to enter Oleshky as localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds
articles.summary: Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky on Friday, a Ukrainian official said, as a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military…

image.caption: A woman walks in front of a damaged residential building in Oleshky, Ukraine, on Wednesday. (Evgeniy Maloletka/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky on Friday, a Ukrainian official said, as a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Military units working to clear landmines as ceasefire stretches into 3rd day

Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, despite remaining locked in war since Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbour more than 4½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
Elsewhere, a jet-powered Russian drone hit two trains stopped at a station in central Ukraine, killing at least 13 people and injuring 10 others, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it in a post on X as a "horrific attack."

items: Russia, Ukraine begin ceasefire in city of Oleshky as deadly strikes continue elsewhere
Trump's increasing support for Russia carries existential danger for Canada

blocks.text: Also, Russia said its air defences downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight, in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
Oleshky ceasefire holds for 54 hours

Both sides thanked U.S. First Lady Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so that food and medical supplies can reach some 2,000 people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.

"The ceasefire has been in place for 54 hours now," Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day. "The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported."
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on de-mining Oleshky roads.

"Both sides are fully honouring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded," she said. "This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."
Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire area expands in eastern Ukraine
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work were unclear.

Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, while Lubinets arrived in Belarus and will head to the city from there, as part of an operation that Lantratova said was five months in the making.
Drone danger in Kherson halts amid truce

The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has also brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
In Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.

"Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn't have under the attacks," she said. "For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop."

The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. "It's a breath of freedom, when you don't look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you're not afraid of dying. It's so great," she said.
"It's such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon."
Russian military personnel pass by damaged vehicle on Wednesday during a de-mining operation they conducted in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky. (Russian Defence Ministry/Reuters)
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favour with Washington ahead of possible talks next month between Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but U.S. President Donald Trump has recently indicated he is disengaging with Kyiv as he waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelenskyy.

Tankers carrying Russian diesel are currently sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will travel to the U.S. for a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Ga., starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow's invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.

Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communications.
Putin said that Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to co-ordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.

"Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius," Putin said late Wednesday. "We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together."

articles.title: Residents of northern Ontario town frustrated with proposed mine that would force them to relocate
articles.summary: If plans to develop a northeastern Ontario mine go ahead, the roughly 500 residents of Virginiatown will need to be relocated to nearby communities.

image.caption: A community centre in Virginiatown was packed with residents concerned about a proposed open pit mine that would force them to relocate. (Jimmy Chabot/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Sudbury·New
If plans to develop a northeastern Ontario mine go ahead, the roughly 500 residents of Virginiatown will need to be relocated to nearby communities.
Cadillac Mines is proposing an open pit mine in Virginiatown that would force a full relocation
Residents learned about the plan when Cadillac Mines CEO Rick Howes said at an investor conference on Sept. 29 that a proposed open pit gold mine would occupy most of the town.

"It's about 250 homes, 500 people. The town has been on a downhill slide since the mine shut down in 1996, so there aren't many services left in town for the people that live there," he said at the meeting. "There's not a lot of opposition as we talk to the community about moving the town."
Around half of Virginiatown's residents were at a public meeting Wednesday evening where the company updated people on its plans.

Leon Leblanc, Cadillac Mines' president and chief operating officer, gave Virginiatown residents more details about a proposed open-pit mine that would occupy a lot of the town's existing footprint. (Jimmy Chabot/Radio-Canada)

“We came in here to apologize. These were obviously comments that were not meant to hurt or to insult anybody,” said Cadillac Mines president and chief operating officer Leon Leblanc, referring to Howes’ earlier comments.
“They were, I think, distasteful, and we're regretting them.”
Leblanc said plans for the proposed mine are early, but if the company were to move ahead, it would require purchasing every home in Virginiatown and resettling everyone.

“We've determined that essentially for the project to be moved up to construction and operation, the impact on McGarry Township is too large and too wide to maintain a portion of the township in place,” he said.
He said the company expects to have more certainty about whether or not it intends to move ahead with the mine by mid-2027.
‘They’re trying to kick us out of our homes’
Residents at the meeting expressed their anger and frustration at the proposed plan and a lack of details so far.
“They're trying to kick us out of our homes,” said Jennifer Tweedy, who recently moved to Virginiatown from the Niagara region.
“My grandmother just moved up here. We're not ready to leave yet. They're going to have to give us more.”
Steve Mallack said even the possibility of a mine forcing everyone to relocate destroys his property value.
“As far as I'm concerned, Cadillac Mines has made Virginiatown a lame duck for selling or buying property,” he said.
Mallack said that for the two years it will take for Cadillac Mines to finalize its plans and determine if it will move ahead with the mine, he will be unable to sell his home.
“Cadillac Mines has made them the only possible buyers for any of the houses in Virginiatown,” he said.
Pat Stevens says she moved to Virginiatown to retire in a more affordable home. Now she's unsure about her future there. (Jimmy Chabot/Radio-Canada)
Pat Stevens said the company’s presentation was vague and didn’t answer her questions.
“I want to be sure that I'm going to be compensated for my moving expenses, for my costs of my home, for the cost of all the repairs I've made to my home,” she said.
“And I would like to guarantee that I will wind up with what I have now, which is a mortgage-free property.”
Stevens said she recently moved to Virginiatown from Grey County, Ont., for the more affordable housing, and to retire.
Because of the lower property values, she said it would be difficult to return to Grey County.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jonathan Migneault is a CBC News reporter based in Sudbury. He is always looking for good stories about northeastern Ontario. Send story ideas to jonathan.migneault@cbc.ca.
With files from Jimmy Chabot

articles.title: Shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?
articles.summary: The US is reportedly considering ways to convert "dark tankers" into legitimate vessels, allowing them to transport crude oil that is not subject to sanctions.

image.caption: To curb Russia's oil export revenues, the US and Europe have stepped up efforts to intercept tankers accused of violating sanctionsImage: Thibaud Moritz/AFP

blocks.text: Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has increasingly relied on a so-called shadow fleet to bypass Western sanctions and transport its oil around the world.
Other heavily sanctioned countries, including Iran and Venezuela, have also been accused of using such vessels to export petroleum products.
These tankers often rely on deceptive practices like turning off their location transponders to evade detection and conceal the cargo's true origins or destinations.

The fleet, which consists largely of aging, uninsured and poorly maintained tankers, has raised widespread concern across the shipping industry. Yet it has expanded rapidly in recent years and now accounts for nearly 19% of global oil tanker capacity, according to estimates by financial intelligence firm S&P Global.

"The shadow fleet is a scourge," Elisabeth Braw, senior fellow at the think tank Atlantic Council, said, adding that "it is in nobody's interest" to have these ships sailing around in the world's oceans.
She pointed out that these tankers undermine the maritime order and increase the risk of accidents and environmental damage.
"Every country should use its leverage with Russia to ask it not to use the fleet," she told DW, noting that ultimately all countries suffer the consequences.
Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it?
Easing sanctions to reduce freight rates?
To clamp down on the fleet and curb Russia's oil export revenues, the United States and European countries have stepped up efforts to intercept tankers accused of violating sanctions.
The Trump administration, however, is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels and allowing them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
A US official told Reuters earlier this month that the move was intended to ease record-high global freight rates.

Lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet "would decrease the effectiveness of the sanctions regime overall," said Michael Carpenter, senior fellow for Transatlantic Affairs at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Such a move "rewards the aggressor and helps Moscow gain revenues to continue attacking Ukraine," he told DW.
"This is the exact opposite of what the US should be doing if it wants to end the war."

Carpenter, who previously served as US ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said any sanctions relief would also put the US and the EU "strategically at odds with each other, with the EU clearly backing Ukraine and the US increasingly supporting Russia's financial goals."
This view is shared by Ben Harris, vice president and director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution.

Lifting sanctions on shadow fleet tankers would "make it substantially easier for Russia to trade its oil at market rates," he said, pointing out that it would "improve its government finances since so much revenue is tied to energy markets."
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, however, rejected suggestions that the US was removing sanctions from shadow fleet tankers.

"We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers," Bloomberg quoted Wright as saying last week. "There is no removing of sanctions," he stressed, adding that the US government was working with investors who buy idle sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
"We're going to move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet,'" Wright said. "They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore."
Is Europe prepared for its next major energy shock?
The US government has yet to unveil a detailed plan for shadow fleet tankers.
Trump's deal with Putin raises concerns
The proposal follows a deal that US President Donald Trump struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin this month to allow sales of Russian diesel onto global markets.
The agreement was seen as part of Trump's efforts to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.

The US president also waived broad new sanctions on Russia authorized by ​a recent legislation, which targeted Moscow's energy revenues and threatened tariffs against the world's largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
The decision was sharply criticized by Ukraine and its European allies over concerns that it could undermine the credibility of sanctions and weaken Western economic pressure on Moscow.
How small waterways make big powers vulnerable
Harris said that "the US sanctions carry outsized weight because of the threat [for countries and businesses] of being cut off from the US financial system."
What can the EU do?

If the US steps away from its sanctions on the shadow fleet, he argued, "the responsibility shifts to European policymakers." Still, they have "less effective options because of the diminished threat of severing financial ties."
Still, the expert stressed that Europe has some tools, pointing to the continent's key role in global shipping and insurance services.

"They can implement measures demanding that tankers carry legitimate and established insurance when traveling through their waters," he said, noting that it "would mean that many shadow fleet tankers could not in practice legally transport Russian oil."
Harris added that European policymakers could also pressure countries worldwide to better regulate the tankers flying their flags.
Carpenter said even if US eases some restrictions, the EU will have no choice but to continue enforcing its sanctions on these vessels.

"The vast majority of the shadow fleet traverses the Baltic Sea and exits it via the Danish Strait," he noted, adding that the EU is "uniquely positioned to board and inspect vessels moving through this key chokepoint."
But Russia has threatened to seize ships belonging to European countries in retaliation for interdicting and seizing Russian vessels suspected of being part of the shadow fleet.
And without US backing, Carpenter said, "it will be harder for EU countries to take on the burdens and risks of sanctions enforcement."

Braw echoed this view, saying that Ukraine's European allies will have to remain united and continue working closely with partners such as Japan, Australia and Canada. Nevertheless, she stressed that what they can achieve on their own "is far less than what they can achieve if the US is part of the team."
What is Russia's shadow fleet doing in the Baltic Sea?

articles.title: Southeast Asian defense ministers aim for proactive engagement amid security threats --Teodoro
articles.summary: Southeast Asian defense ministers have agreed to be more proactive in engaging as security threats become more unpredictable, said Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 8:00pm

Southeast Asian defense ministers have agreed to be more proactive in engaging as security threats become more unpredictable, said Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Thursday.

“I think what is also significant is that defense leaders realize that security threats are becoming more unpredictable,” he said during a press briefing at the sidelines of ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu.

“I think there is unanimous consensus that ASEAN defense ministers meet and the plus must be more proactive in engaging and hopefully more participative in engaging in the number of fields or topics that we discuss, we study together,” he added.
During the meeting, the Philippine defense chief said that ASEAN defense leaders adopted several initiatives.

“These include principally promoting exchanges among our younger and upcoming defense leaders and military leaders, strengthening our individual and collective resilience against chemical, biological, and radiological threats,” said Teodoro.
Moreover, Teodoro said that there is no such thing as “quick wins” in dealing with security issues.
“Well, we don't have quick wins in ASEAN. It is a process of engaging because it is a consensus-based organization,” he said.
The Philippines is hosting the 20th ADMM and the 13th ADMM-Plus on October 28 and 29 inCebu.
ADMM is ASEAN's highest defense consultative and cooperative mechanism, according to the Department of National Defense (DND).
The ADMM-Plus expands defense cooperation to eight dialogue partners including Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: 'More than courteous' for undersecretary to meet defense attache --Teodoro
articles.summary: DND Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said it"s “more than courteous” that another department executive has welcomed China"s defense attache during the ADMM-Plus meeting in Cebu.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 7:48pm

Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said on Thursday that it’s “more than courteous” that it was another department executive who welcomed China’s defense attaché during the meeting among Southeast Asian defense ministers in Cebu.

“Well, there should be some parity in rank and in stature. So, I think an undersecretary receiving an attaché, that is already more than courteous,” said Teodoro during a press briefing at the sidelines of ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus).

Teodoro personally welcomed, shook hands, and took photos with defense ministers and representatives of other countries when they entered the venue earlier in the day, except China’s defense attaché to the Philippines Senior Captain Yang Lei.
China has banned Teodoro from entering its territory, and its diplomats have accused him of being "anti-China."

Tensions between Manila and Beijing continue over the contested South China Sea. Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory are referred to as the West Philippine Sea by the government.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.

In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines, invalidating China’s sweeping claims over much of the South China Sea and finding no legal basis for its claim to historic rights within the so-called nine-dash line.
Moreover, Teodoro denied the latest accusation that the Philippines, which hosts the ADMM-Plus meeting, has obstructed China’s participation in the meet.
“Insofar as ASEAN is concerned, I do not believe our ASEAN member countries feel that way. If not, they would have let me know,” said Teodoro.
“So it is China's position, it is not ASEAN's position,” he added.
Teodoro made the response after Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson Zhang Xiaogang reportedly said that Philippines’ actions as ADMM-Plus chair undermined the inclusivity of the meet.

“No country has the right to characterize ASEAN processes except ASEAN member countries. They are dialogue partners. So as much as we would want to accommodate them, it is subject to rules and limitations,” Teodoro further responded. — BM, GMA News
