articles.title: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.summary: Xi's anti-corruption campaign has become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", observers say.

blocks.text: Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."

In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollwed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 34 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.

Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.

The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.

Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-men Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."

articles.title: Ukraine: 13 killed in Russian drone strike on crowded Dnipro train station
articles.summary: A jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform at a civilian station in Dnipro, killing and injuring passengers who were waiting to board a train. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy called the attack…

image.caption: The strike hit a crowded train platform during the morning rush hour Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least 13 people were killed and five more injured when a Russian drone struck a passenger train which was stopped at a station in the eastern Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday morning.

According to Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, a jet-powered drone struck a platform on which people were waiting to board a regional train to Zaporizhzhia, about a two-hour journey to the south.
"Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said.
Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three drones in the daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them.
Dnipro city mayor Borys Filatov also confirmed the incident, which he called a "tragedy."
Zelenskyy issues veiled Trump criticism after 'horrific' attack
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific" and demanded international action from Kyiv's allies.
"Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he said.

"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating?" he asked, referring to a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin which saw some sanctions on Russia eased in exchange for the release of Russian diesel stocks onto global markets.
French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his "deep concern" that Russia continues to "opt for escalation" by targeting civilians.

"In this context, we must aim for much more than a localized ceasefire — such as the one recently negotiated for Oleshky," the French president said on social media, describing Moscow’s rejection of "all proposals to that end" as "intolerable."
"Together, we must redouble our efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace and bring Russia to the negotiating table," he said.
DW witnesses Ukrainian train evacuation
How Russia targets Ukrainian trains
Russia has been targeting Ukrainian trains and stations since day one of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing railway workers and passengers.
Faced with an increasing number of Russian drone attacks, Ukrainian trains began large-scale passenger evacuations this year — often while trains are already mid-journey.
In September alone, more than 5,800 trains had to be evacuated due to the threat of strikes, Ukrzaliznytsia told the AFP news agency.
Most evacuations take place in regions near the front line, in the south and east of the country: in Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia.
When a potential Russian strike is detected, the train comes to a halt and passengers are required to leave their carriages and wait at a safe distance until the danger has passed.
With commercial air travel in Ukraine shut down due to the war, the country's vast railway network has become essential for transporting people and goods, as well as for entering and leaving Ukraine.
Ukraine's unbreakable line: Trains to the frontline
Ukraine: More Russian attacks
Also on Thursday, authorities reported at least five other fatalities resulting from other Russian attacks across Ukraine.

articles.title: Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
articles.summary: The Republican governor was responding to allegations in the New York Times that Democrats recruited a spoiler candidate, Dan Sullivan.

blocks.text: The Republican governor of Alaska has ordered an investigation into an alleged "scheme" designed "to manipulate Alaska's elections".

Governor Mike Dunleavy said he was responding to a New York Times (NYT) report, external. The story said the team of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked with people who tried to recruit a man to contest the Senate race who shares their name with Peltola's opponent, Dan Sullivan.
Sullivan, the incumbent senator, and fellow Republicans have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be barred.
Peltola's team deny any wrongdoing, or encouraging the second Dan Sullivan to stand in the tight contest.

For his part, the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, denies any links with the Peltola campaign. Although he has given few interviews, he told the NYT, external in August he was running the race in good faith as a moderate Republican, albeit that he had voted for Peltola in previous contests.
The ballot paper is set to list the two men as Dan S Sullivan, who will be described as the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Senator Dan Sullivan told Fox News on Wednesday night that Peltola should "come clean" and described it as a scandal of the highest order.
His fellow Republican senator in Alaska, Lisa Murkowksi, accused the Democratic campaign of engaging in a "pattern of lies".

The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Americans head to the polls across the country on Tuesday.
Previous efforts by the Republicans to remove that Sullivan, the retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.
But Dunleavy's statement, which did not name the Peltola campaign, said the NYT reporting had supported findings by the state Division of Elections earlier this year.

"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," he wrote. "The evidence will determine what happens next."

The NYT report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Sullivan the schoolteacher to stand in the Senate race.
This was part of a broader effort to encourage other would-be "spoiler" candidates to enter the race and dilute the support of the sitting Republican senator, the newspaper reported.

The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the NYT's reporting.

In a series of Truth Social posts, Trump too pointed to the report and made a variety of allegations against Peltola, who he argued should be removed from the ballot. He repeated his endorsement for Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator, writing: "Dan is a GREAT man, has ALWAYS delivered for Alaska."

His administration previously filed a legal case aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed candidate loses, arguing that the presence of both Sullivans on the ballot could confuse voters.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.

The battle threatens to delay the full picture of nationwide results following the midterm elections. The ultimate question of which party controls Congress will have a significant bearing on the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.

articles.title: US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over DR Congo conflict
articles.summary: Congo accuses Rwanda of backing M23 rebels and plundering minerals in its conflict hit East

blocks.text: The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its alleged support for the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing pressure on Kigali to withdraw its troops and halt support for the rebels.
"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict.
Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. Rwanda denies backing M23.
The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.

The M23 has seized mineral-rich areas, including gold-mining sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area in North Kivu. Washington says minerals from rebel-held territory enter Rwanda's supply chains, alleging that Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.

The sanctions are intended to reinforce the Washington Accords, signed by the Congolese and Rwandan presidents in December 2025 under US mediation. The deal aimed to end the conflict and expand regional trade and investment, but fighting has continued.
On 24 October, ahead of the sanctions announcement, DR Congo President Félix Tshisekedi urged the international community to increase pressure on Rwanda.
"We must firmly demand that the international community impose concrete sanctions against Rwanda and exert increased pressure, so that we may finally secure a lasting peace in our country," he said.

In a statement to Reuters, DR Congo foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and urged Rwanda to honour its commitments under the Washington Accords, respect the UN Charter and withdraw its troops from Congolese territory.

"The Washington Accords contain clear commitments regarding Rwanda's security, specifically the neutralization of the DR Congo-sponsored FDLR genocidal militia, which are wholly unmet, and with no accountability," Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo told the BBC.
The FDLR is a militia linked to perpetrators of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Kigali considers it a security threat and cites its presence in eastern DR Congo to justify its military posture.

"Rwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable," she said.
The US also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a popular bank and financial institution serving Rwanda's security services.

Washington alleges it facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, helped pay for military equipment for Rwandan forces from China and enabled gold to be transported from rebel-controlled areas to Kigali.

The sanctions freeze the designated entities' assets under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with them, unless authorised or exempt. Violations can result in penalties for US and foreign parties.

The measures follow earlier US sanctions against Rwanda's army and four senior military commanders in March 2026. The US imposed further sanctions on Gasabo gold refinery and three mining companies accused of smuggling conflict minerals in June 2026.

Pressure is also mounting over Rwanda's international sports partnerships. Two US senators have urged the National Basketball Association (NBA) to reconsider its commercial relations with Kigali, questioning whether it aligns with the league's stated commitment to human rights.

In a letter sent to NBA commissioner Adam Silver on 23 October, senators Jeff Merkley and Marsha Blackburn questioned the league's continued partnership with Rwanda amid allegations of human rights abuses.
The NBA has yet to issue a substantive response to the letter.
Rwanda has used sports high-profile sports sponsorship to raise its international profile. Early this month, it secured a 10-year deal to host Formula 1's African Grand Prix in the early 2030s.
The country's sponsorship of Arsenal ended in 2026, while Bayern Munich has also ended its commercial partnership with Visit Rwanda.

The M23 has recently joined a new rebel coalition, known as the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) and led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, which wants to oust Tshisekedi's government.

articles.title: ECB President Lagarde resigns at time of mounting challenges for Europe
articles.summary: A source with direct knowledge of the matter says Christine Lagarde resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally

blocks.text: Jana Rodenbusch/Reuters
A source with direct knowledge of the matter says Christine Lagarde resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally

items: Christine Lagarde announced her resignation as European Central Bank President, effective February 7, amid rising economic volatility in Europe.
Her departure allows EU leaders to select a successor, with Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos seen as frontrunners.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

FRANKFURT, Germany – European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Thursday, October 29, ending months of speculation about her future just as Europe enters a period of rising economic volatility and divisive electoral politics.

Lagarde will step down on February 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favored to win.
The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.
“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a short video shared on social media.

A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution’s independence.

European Council President Antonio Costa said in a statement the process to find a successor for Lagarde would begin immediately. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as frontrunners.
“The rumored successors are both very competent, well-established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much,” Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.
Financial markets did not move much after the announcement, with some analysts noting the ECB had by now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.

“The ECB is now quite well-established, the market is familiar with the way it operates,” Goldman Sachs’ head of Fixed Income Macro Investing Simon Dangoor said. “Our view is that institutional behavior is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over.”
Lagarde’s term was scheduled to run until the end of October 2027, but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination.
The ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.

But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.

Caught between persistent inflation fueled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday while signaling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.

“There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB’s inflation forecast due to higher energy prices,” Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.
The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 1315 GMT on Thursday, followed by Lagarde’s regular press conference at 1345 GMT.

Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.
The more immediate challenge for policymakers may be turmoil in bond markets.

A global rise in yields, fueled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.

In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country’s growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following this year’s elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.

The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs. France is now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt over benchmark German bonds is larger than for any other euro zone country.
That has fueled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.
“They’ve typically come up with a new tool that’s customised for that specific set of circumstances,” said Dangoor at Goldman Sachs.
The ECB’s first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programs of the previous decade.
Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure. – Rappler.com

Former president says ‘these are not serious people’ as Trump holds rallies for Republican candidates

Around lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of…

blocks.text: Trump and Obama trade barbs in closing week of US midterm election
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Trump and the former president Barack Obama have continued to trade barbs on the campaign trail, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.

While Donald Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz ⁠that has exposed Republican concerns about losing control of ⁠Congress for the final two years of his presidency, ​Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week.

However, the former Democratic president has taken a more prominent role in recent days, delivering speeches criticizing Trump, which appear to have got under the skin of the current occupant of the White House.

“These are not serious people,” he said of Donald Trump and the Republican party, speaking at a Wednesday campaign rally in suburban Atlanta. “And we’re all paying the price for their lack of seriousness.”
Obama has offered pointed criticism of Republican candidates and Donald Trump in a style that has been unusual for the former president.

He continued to do so on Wednesday, again invoking the image of Trump’s gilded renovations of the White House and noting Trump’s strident reaction to his crack last week likening it to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.

“The Saddam Hussein thing didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. “I mean, it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part: they mobilized a whole government response to that joke.

“The White House even called the secretary of the treasury,” the former president continued. “The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation … they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”
Trump, meanwhile, defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated.

“The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” ⁠he said at a rally in Ohio.

Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest ⁠for the Senate seen as very close.

blocks.text: Judge rebuffs Trump DoJ’s bid to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots

blocks.caption: Sam Levine

blocks.text: Sam Levine

A federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.

The ruling from US district judge David Carter, nominated to the federal bench by Bill Clinton, comes about two weeks after the justice department delivered a USB drive to election officials in Los Angeles and Sacramento that it said contained the names of 20,000 non-citizens on the state’s voter rolls. There are more than 23 million registered voters in California and non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

“This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election,” Carter wrote in his Wednesday evening ruling. “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign,” Carter continued. “But California and its people are sovereign, too.”

The justice department gave officials just 48 hours to review the list and said it would sue the state if officials did not sequester ballots from those whose citizenship it could not confirm. The department refused to provide more details about its methodology and Los Angeles officials found preliminary indicators the list was inaccurate. The justice department then sued California on 15 October to try and force the state to sequester the ballots and verify citizenship.
How did the Cheesecake Factory end up in a Maga fight over ‘elitism’?

blocks.caption: Matthew Cantor

blocks.text: Matthew Cantor

Around lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.
Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.
The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.

It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.

Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.
Then the backlash began.

articles.title: Spanish rescue workers search for any survivors in high-speed rail crash, with 69 dead
articles.summary: Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, in which one train struck another from behind, killing 69 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network ahead of…

image.caption: Investigators work Thursday amongst debris and damaged carriages of a train crash between two high-speed trains around 150 kilometres south of Madrid between Urda and Los Yebenes in the province of Toledo, Spain, a day after the accident. (Oscar Del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, in which one train struck another from behind, killing 69 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network ahead of a national election.
Death toll could rise, officials say, as Canadian government monitors 7 citizens affected by crash

Search teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims on Thursday morning, a day after the collision in central Spain. Cranes helped shift the carriages as police and soldiers helped pick through the wreckage strewn down the gravel slope where at least three train carriages were tossed by the impact.
Officials have said the death toll was provisional. One more body was found overnight, taking the death toll to 69, according to the regional leader of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page.
"Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock," García-Page said.

García-Page said that a crane would lift a damaged carriage that had flipped over. He added that 50 people remained hospitalized. "Besides bodies, there are body parts that need to be identified," García-Page said.
Spain's government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday.
High-speed train crash in Spain kills dozens, Canadians among the injured

Global Affairs Canada (GAC) told CBC News on Wednesday that it is aware of six Canadians who were injured in the crash, and a seventh person was unaccounted for. The severity of injuries was not clear, with the department citing privacy considerations.

"Our thoughts are with their families and loved ones as well as all of those affected," the GAC statement said. "Canadian officials are providing consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities to gather more information."
Calls for transport minister to resign

Spain's high-speed rail network has been considered one of the nation's crowning achievements. It is the world's second-largest, after China's. Until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service more than three decades ago.
Forty-six people died in a January crash when one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.

Members of Spain's Military Emergency Unit are shown Thursday near a tent set up next to the Institute of Forensic Medicine following the train collision in Toledo. (Andrea Comas/The Associated Press)

Both deadly crashes this year took place on the same rail line. Each involved a train operated by state-owned RENFE and another operated by privately owned IRYO. Spain liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente faced media questions over whether he would resign following a second major train wreck under his watch. He said he was fully focused on dealing with the collision, not his future.

Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command centre for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. local time the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometres stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped near the town of Urda, while the RENFE train was 25 kilometres behind it.
But a few minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.

Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Thousands of travellers were left stranded and searching for alternative transport after the high-speed line connecting Madrid and Seville was shut down.
Crash becomes another issue on campaign trail
The collision Wednesday morning that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site in the province of Toledo on Wednesday. He pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy.

"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sánchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."

items: How did Spain's housing crisis get so bad it forced the PM to call a snap election?
Spanish pensioner Maricarmen, symbol of country's housing crisis, dead at 87

blocks.text: Sánchez has weathered many crises since taking power in 2018, but polls show he and his Socialists faces another uphill battle when voters cast ballots in Spain's first national election in more than three years, on Nov. 29.

Discontent over housing costs and high rents led to the early election call. Sánchez now also faces questions about the safety of Spain's rail service along with criticism from right-wing parties of his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny.

Sánchez's main rival, People's Party Leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash on Wednesday. The conservative leader said that in respect for the victims his party cancelled its campaign events for the day.
The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.
"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No report of Indonesian President confronting, scolding Marcos
articles.summary: The video contains no footage, audio, or documentation of the alleged confrontation. Instead, the content features an unidentified male commentator reacting to a third-party social media post…

blocks.text: Claim: Indonesia’s president publicly confronted and scolded President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., telling him to “fix yourself and your country.”

Why we fact-checked this: The YouTube channel “PINAS BALITA TV” with 175,000 subscribers published a video bearing the title: “GRABE NA! NAKAKAH1YA TO! IND0NESIAN PRESIDENT HARAPANG SINUP4L-P4L at NA-REALTALK si BEBE EM?” (This is too much! How embarrassing! Indonesian President confronted and engaged BBM in real talk?)
The video’s thumbnail, posted on October 17, 2026, shows an enraged Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto pointing directly at the President’s face before press microphones and cameras.

In the video’s original thumbnail, the uploader claimed that the Indonesian leader told Marcos to “fix your country and yourself,” though this line has since been edited out as of writing.As of writing, the video has garnered 3,100 views and 234 likes.

The facts: No credible news reports or official footage confirm that Indonesia’s Subianto confronted or publicly engaged Marcos in real talk before the press.AI image detectors IsThisAI reveal that the thumbnail of the video is 99% likely to be AI-generated. Meanwhile, SightEngine flagged it as 87% likely to have used generative AI, and TruthScan estimated an 85% edit probability with high confidence.“The background crowd appears to be cloned or manipulated, showing unnatural repetition patterns. Shadows on the subjects’ faces and clothing are inconsistent, further suggesting digital editing,” the TruthScan findings said.

Lack of evidence: The video contains no footage, audio, or documentation of any confrontation. Instead, the content features an unidentified male commentator reacting to a third-party social media post.

The commentator compares how both governments address climate challenges — particularly El Niño — contrasting Indonesia’s reported distribution of water pumps with the Philippine government’s recommendation to collect rainwater using buckets. The commentator heavily criticized the administration’s suggested solution.Existing ties: Diplomatic ties between the Philippines and Indonesia remain stable as of writing. Both countries held bilateral meetings in 2024, and Marcos, along with First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, formally welcomed President Subianto during the opening ceremony of the 48th ASEAN Summit held in Cebu in May 2026.
Marcos also traveled to Jakarta to attend Subianto’s presidential inauguration in 2024.
Debunked: Marcos has been a frequent subject of false claims, particularly controversies:

FACT CHECK: Marcos statement claiming to cancel 2028 election is taken out of context
FACT CHECK: Marcos Jr. did not say protecting VP Duterte from her case is ‘corruption’
FACT CHECK: Marcos did not say he wants another 6-year presidential term

articles.title: Rare love letters to French aristocrat shed light on Louis XVI maritime mystery
articles.summary:
‘Miracle’ cache of letters written by French scientist who died in ill-fated La Pérouse mission give personal account of 1785 voyage

As he prepared to climb the scaffolding to be publicly…

blocks.text: As he prepared to climb the scaffolding to be publicly executed by guillotine on 21 January 1793, Louis XVI is reported to have asked: “Is there news of Monsieur de la Pérouse?”

He was referring to Jean-François de Galaup, the count of Pérouse, a naval officer and navigator whom the French king had dispatched in 1785 on a round-the-world scientific mission to rival discoveries made by the English explorer Captain James Cook.

blocks.caption: The veiled love letters sent by Jean-André Mongez to Louise Victoire Le Cloustier were discovered in a book of engravings. Photograph: Daguerre Paris

blocks.text: The two ships under La Pérouse’s command, La Boussole and L’Astrolabe, disappeared three years later after leaving Botany Bay in Australia. The wrecks were only formally identified in 2005 and exactly what happened to them remains a mystery to this day.

Now rare letters written by an illustrious scientist who perished in 1788 have resurfaced, giving a new and personal account of the voyage. They are described as veiled love letters addressed to the married daughter of an aristocratic family, and were discovered hidden in a book of engravings being examined in preparation for auction.
Ludovic Miran, a book and manuscript expert for the auctioneers selling the letters next month, described the find as “a miracle”.

“We have a certain number of documents from the expedition but they are almost all scientific, so these personal letters are extremely rare,” Miran told the Guardian. “They throw a completely new light on what is in France an extraordinary scientific and historical event.”

The La Pérouse expedition was launched at a time when Britain and France were in a period of intense rivalry over colonial expansion. La Pérouse was a great admirer of Cook and his maritime mapping and scientific discoveries, but Louis XVI had more political and trade ambitions. The French wanted to create trade routes and discover whether the secret information they had that Britain was planning to establish a permanent base at Botany Bay, giving it access to unexplored areas of the Pacific region, was correct.

La Pérouse’s ships, carrying 225 crew officers and scientists, sailed from Brest on France’s Atlantic coast on 1 August 1785 and for almost three years sent reports during stopovers including from Alaska, California, Asia, Russia and Samoa, where the captain of the Astrolabe and 11 men were killed.

At the time of Louis XVI’s execution, there had been no news of the frigates since their departure from Botany Bay in March 1788. To La Pérouse’s dismay, Captain Arthur Phillip and Britain’s First Fleet had beaten him to the Australian coast – inhabited by an Indigenous population for tens of thousands of years – by just six days.

blocks.caption: A map of the voyage taken by La Boussole and L’Astrolabe, an expedition commissioned by Louis XVI. Photograph: Daguerre Paris

blocks.text: La Boussole and L’Astrolabe are believed to have foundered on coral reefs at Vanikoro east of the Solomon Islands during a tornado a few months later. Wreckage was discovered in 1826 and 1964 but only formally identified in 2005.

The letters were written by Jean-André Mongez, a brilliant scientist, director of an illustrious science revue and church canon who was with the expedition, to Louise Victoria Le Cloustier, the daughter of a minor noble family from Rouen, Normandy.

Miran said Mongez used the letters to express his unhappiness at her marriage and appears to repent for previous bad behaviour. “He writes several times: ‘I will be back, I will be another man, a better man’,” Miran said. “One has the impression he has not behaved well towards her and she has put him in his place.”

blocks.caption: Captain Arthur Phillip raises a British flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788. Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty

blocks.text: This may, he added, have been behind Mongez’s decision to undertake such a long and perilous journey. “The references are often veiled, but they seem to have had a very close relationship but he seems to have caused some offence at some point. They are intimate, very personal letters,” he said.

“He tells her he is leaving ‘a bit for the love of fame and the desire to acquire new knowledge’, but he already had scientific glory and a good career and they would have all read James Cook’s works before leaving so they knew about the dangers.
after newsletter promotion
“We will never know why he decided to join this perilous journey, but it is clear he was leaving in part because of this emotional relationship.”

Miran added: “The correspondence also provides answers as to how these young men endured three years of navigation around the world, a completely new and unimaginable experience. We learn how they withstood the shock of such a crazy journey and horrible conditions.

“He recounts how his friend and others were massacred on one stop. In his last letter he tells her the expedition has taken a sad turn and he now only wants to come home because such unhappiness is not compensated for by the meagre scientific results they have.
“Perhaps it is a journey of redemption.”

blocks.caption: The letters, valued at €30,000-€50,000, are being sold at auction in Paris. Photograph: Daguerre Paris

blocks.text: Le Cloustier died in 1821, like the rest of the world unaware of the fate of Mongez or the expedition. “But she kept the letters and we can tell they have been read, and reread. I would imagine she had to hide them from her husband,” Miran said.
The auctioneer Benoît Derouineau said he had discovered the letters in an “unremarkable” 19th-century book of engravings being prepared for sale.

“I didn’t realise what they were at first. They had clearly been carefully saved and hidden. Perhaps because they were a kind of love letter and the recipient didn’t want them seen. But she hadn’t thrown them away or burned them,” he said.
“That Louis XVI is said to have asked about La Pérouse shows how much was invested in this expedition. It was a very important event in France.”
The letters, valued at €30,000-€50,000, are being sold as one lot by Daguerre at the Hôtel Drouot, Paris, on 17 November.

articles.title: Europe’s central bank chief Christine Lagarde to step down nine months early
articles.summary:
Departure of Lagarde, seen as candidate to take over World Economic Forum, comes as eurozone struggles with weak growth and inflation

Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, is…

blocks.text: Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, is stepping down nine months early, ending months of speculation about her future.
The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday morning that Lagarde would step down as its president on 7 February 2027; her term was scheduled to run until the end of October next year.
The ECB’s governing council thanked Lagarde warmly and gave her a long standing ovation, as it met to set interest rates across the eurozone.

Lagarde has been seen as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct – which he denies.

Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is strugging with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.

“The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027,” said Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Elysee Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”

Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the ECB has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Middle East conflict and Donald Trump’s trade war.
The ECB is widely expected to keep interest rates on hold on Thursday afternoon.

articles.title: Sandro's budget insertions? Palace says public funds must be utilized properly
articles.summary: The Palace emphasized that all of the projects to be funded by the 2027 national budget should have the proper details, saying that President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. will look at everything…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 6:47pm

The Palace emphasized that all of the projects to be funded by the 2027 national budget should have the proper details, saying that President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. will look at everything properly with no exception—including those linked to his son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro addressed the budget insertions being linked to Sandro Marcos, saying that any insinuations were premature, as the budget still needed to go through the entire legislative process.
However, no project should be approved that lacked details, she stressed.

“Ang pondo ng bayan ay dapat pakinabangan ng sambayanan, iyan ang utos ng Pangulo. Kung may kailangan na mabigay na mga detalye, hindi—uulitin ko po, itong aking pagsagot ay hindi lamang para sa isyu ni Congressman Sandro Marcos; ito po ay sa lahat ng mga mambabatas na siyang mayroong power of the purse,” Castro said.

(Public funds must be used by the public, that is the President’s orders. If details need to be given, no—I will say it again, my answer is not just Congressman Sandro Marcos’ issue; this is for all of the lawmakers with the power of the purse.)

“Hindi po pipikitan ng Pangulo ang mga proyektong alam nilang walang detalye. So, doon po sa mga nagbabantay sa budget, kailangan namin ang tulong ninyo. Hindi po kayo makakasira sa gobyerno. Kapag may nakita po kayo na dapat tapikin, na dapat pagtuunan ng pansin, sabihin lang po ninyo at nakikinig ang Pangulo,” she added.

(The President will now close his eyes on any project that lacks details. So to those who are guarding the budget, we need your help. You will not be wrecking the government. If you see something that should be hit, that should be given notice, you should say it and the President is listening.)
Castro also thumbed down several headlines that made it appear like she was defending the congressman.

The People’s Budget Coalition said it found more than P1 trillion worth of "red flags" in the proposed 2027 budget, and alleged that the largest chunk of infrastructure insertions—P4.37 billion—has been allotted to Sandro Marcos’ district. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Germany news: Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom
articles.summary: Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said North Korea is putting Europe's security at risk by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in Ukraine. DW has more.

image.caption: North Korea is thought to have sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight for RussiaImage: Korean Central News Agency/YONHAPNEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 29, 2026
Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz met with President Lee Jae Myung Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."
North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.
In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.
Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.
At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.
The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.

articles.title: SWS survey reflects Senate impeachment court's fair procedure --Tongol
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Thursday committed to continue having a “transparent, rules-based impartiality” in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 6:22pm

The Senate impeachment court on Thursday committed to continue having a “transparent, rules-based impartiality” in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, following a recent Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey.

The survey showed that 51% of adult Filipinos agreed that the Senate decision—whether the Vice President is acquitted or convicted—should be accepted. Meanwhile, 26% (correctly rounded) disagreed, and 24% were undecided.
Impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said that they see such numbers with “both quiet confidence in its even-handed procedure and a sober resolve to earn the trust of a cautious public.”

“Rather than treating these numbers with complacency, the Impeachment Court views the remaining undecided and skeptical segments of the public as a continuing challenge to demonstrate transparent, rules-based impartiality,” he said in a statement.

“As the proceedings resume on November 9, 2026, for the presentation of the Respondent’sevidence on Article II, the Senate Impeachment Court will continue to enforce the rules of evidence and accord full due process to both sides, ensuring that its final constitutional judgment commands the respect of the entire nation,” he added.

He also stressed that while the court welcomes public attentiveness to the impeachment trial, the survey metrics only measure public sentiment, while senator-judges “are bound by oath to render judgment strictly on the basis of law and admissible evidence.”

The same SWS survey revealed that 35% of adult Filipinos are dissatisfied, while 30% are satisfied "that the prosecution of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte is being done in a just manner.”

The non-commissioned survey was conducted from September 21 to 27, 2026, using face-to-face interviews of 1,500 adults aged 18 years old and above nationwide. The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages, ±4% for Balance Luzon, and ±6% each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount
articles.summary: A ship in the Strait of Hormuz is reported to be on fire, a British maritime agency says. Iran has meanwhile said it has shot down another US drone as military tensions with Washington continue.

image.caption: Another ship is reportedly on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, seen here from OmanImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: A ship on fire has been reported in the Strait of Hormuz, British maritime agency UKMTO said on Thursday.
The agency, which is run by the British Royal Navy, did not give details on the cause of the blaze or any casualties.
Iran has, however, recently stepped up its attacks on ships that it sees as using the waterway without proper authorization.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route, but it is not known if the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them.
This comes as Iran has reported shooting down another US drone east of the waterway as fears grow of a new escalation in the US-Iran war.
Iran steps up attacks in Strait of Hormuz
The UKMTO said the captain of another ship had reported the blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, which is located just off the strait.
The status of ⁠the ​crew is ​unknown, and so far ​no information has emerged pertaining to ⁠damage or environmental ⁠impact.

Since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers to be unauthorized users of the waterway.
Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler.
Attacks on ships in the strait are at the highest level since the war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.

blocks.caption: The Strait of Hormuz is a vital chokepoint for oil and gas transportImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: US drone downed
The reported ship fire comes as Iran says its forces have downed a drone near the strait, with the Tasnim news agency citing the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used.
The report said that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out.
The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.

blocks.caption: The MQ-1 Predator can be used both for surveillance and attackImage: Col. Leslie Pratt/epa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fears of new US strikes
The latest incidents come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen to be considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Last week, Trump said, "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war. He did not, however, give any timeframe.
A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region.
As reports of a possible renewed escalation swirl, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly nonetheless fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia.

If confirmed, the ouster would be the latest in a series of such high-level departures under the Trump administration, with Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee being forced to retire last October.
According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.

articles.title: [READOUT] How can businesses win back customers amid a weak peso and high inflation?
articles.summary: Businesses must balance rising costs against the dwindling purchasing power and growing frustration of cash-strapped consumers

blocks.text: What can businesses do to win over customers already struggling with high prices? An October study by Organic Intelligence suggests a concrete response some brands could consider.

Asked what would make a brand feel genuinely on their side, the top response was a price freeze (27%), ahead of smaller tingi sizes (16%), free shipping (14%), and promotional bundles (12%). The study’s researchers later told Rappler that a price freeze campaign would be highly effective in building customer loyalty with value-conscious customers.

The findings reflect how financially stretched consumers have become. The survey of 800 urban Filipinos, conducted in May, also found that 42% had borrowed for essentials such as food and transportation, while 45% said inflation had drained their motivation to get ahead.
And the pressure is unlikely to ease in the near-term. September inflation reached 7.2%, with further acceleration expected when October figures come out on November 5.
Meanwhile, businesses must weigh consumer sentiment against how much of their rising costs they can realistically pass on to consumers.

The peso closed at another historic low of P64.17 to the dollar on Tuesday, October 27, despite the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) delivering a larger-than-expected 50 basis point rate hike just five days earlier. That brought its policy rate to 5.50%, following four consecutive increases this year.

After the same Monetary Board meeting, the BSP raised its 2027 inflation forecast from 5.4% to 6%, signaling that businesses may have to contend with higher costs and weaker consumer purchasing power for longer.

The BSP, however, is in no hurry to defend the peso at any particular exchange rate. Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said the central bank would largely let the currency find its own level, intervening only to cushion excessive movements that could worsen inflation.

Former BSP deputy governor Diwa Guinigundo pointed to deeper problems behind the peso’s slide, including weak capital flows, the country’s balance of payments deficit, low foreign investment, and investor uncertainty surrounding corruption allegations and the ongoing messy impeachment trial.
Consider the numbers:

items: The Philippines recorded a $9.1-billion balance of payments deficit in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $5.3 billion a year earlier. Foreign portfolio investments registered $4.25 billion in net outflows from January to August, reversing $4.58 billion in inflows a year earlier.

The country’s hefty import bill also creates enormous demand for dollars. Consider that imports of mineral fuels and related products alone increased by $2.56 billion year on year in the first half of 2026.
And the pressure could persist. The BSP forecasts another $8.5-billion balance of payments deficit in 2027, alongside a $19.4-billion current account deficit.

Foreign exchange reserves, meanwhile, fell from $104.8 billion in August to $99.5 billion in September, partly due to BSP foreign exchange operations, valuation adjustments, and government withdrawals. Still, those reserves are enough to cover 6.2 months of import.

blocks.text: How this affects businesses depends on which side of the dollar they sit.

Import-dependent manufacturers, retailers, airlines, and companies with unhedged dollar debt face higher costs. Exporters and business process outsourcing firms earning dollars while paying expenses in pesos could benefit from the exchange rate. Higher interest rates, meanwhile, make new borrowing and refinancing costlier, adding pressure to firms already struggling with input costs.

Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. says prolonged inflation may pose a greater threat to economic growth than higher interest rates, especially with household consumption accounting for around 70% of the economy.
Looking ahead, the November 9 third quarter 2026 GDP release will be the next measure to watch after economic growth slowed to a disappointing 2.3% in the second quarter of 2026.
Yet difficult economic conditions have not stopped companies from raising capital.

GCash parent Mynt completed the largest IPO in Philippine history on October 20, with the Philippine Stock Exchange reporting a P60.9-billion offering, including the overallotment. Meanwhile, Cebu-based Aznar Shipping is set to launch a smaller IPO of up to P737 million, targeting a December 18 listing to finance fleet and shipyard expansion.
We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.

articles.title: Edmonton and Calgary rejected her referendum. Does Danielle Smith have a city problem?
articles.summary: Nowhere in Alberta was the idea of a second referendum less popular than in urban centres. A year out from an election, Premier Danielle Smith says she's committed to identifying the issues important…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith must contend with a sizable group of urban Albertans who appear to have rejected her latest political project, while she publicly spars with councillors over local issues such as zoning. (Sean Kilpatrick/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: This week the Alberta government pivots back to governing, with MLAs returning to the legislature for the first time since a contentious referendum on separation exposed the divide between, among other things, urban and rural Albertans.

Much of the pushback on the 10 referendum questions came from the province’s two largest centres. Calgary collectively voted "no" on all questions except proof of citizenship to vote, while Edmonton was a "no" across the board. Nowhere was the prospect of a second separation vote less popular.
“We all know there’s an urban-rural divide in Alberta politics,” says Lisa Young, a political scientist at the University of Calgary. “But the referendum results make it really stark.”

This presents a quandary for Premier Danielle Smith, who has historically been supported by — and focused her attention on — rural Alberta. Now, she must contend with a sizable group of urban Albertans who appear to have rejected her latest political project, while she publicly spars with councillors over local issues such as zoning.

Meanwhile, it remains to be seen whether her list of priorities for the upcoming sitting, which include public sector hiring based on "merit," protections for data centre development and the future of bike lanes, will speak to the cities.
“I think a lot of the recent focus on the more performative politics has served the UCP minority base really well,” said Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas on Tuesday.

“But the more we debate … which books should be in a library,” he said, referring to a recent bill to limit sexually explicit material in public libraries, “the more you lose the mainstream Calgarians who actually just want to get things done, want to know that life is safe and affordable.”

Smith herself has talked about the need to refocus on voters in Edmonton and Calgary, telling CBC News last week that her government needed to “identify the issues” that were important to residents of the two urban centres, which together make up just over half of the provincial population.

items: Danielle Smith has said no to a second referendum. But that decision might not be hers to make
Fight for independence won't end after referendum: Alberta Prosperity Project leader

blocks.text: Urban voters are focused on issues like education, health care and affordability, which is why her government has (temporarily) paused the gas tax at the pumps and rolled out “complexity teams” in classrooms, Smith said.

“The issues that were of the referendum, I think it’s pretty clear those are ... of greater interest to those who are in political parties and punditry circles and in rural Alberta than they were in Calgary or Edmonton."
Mapping out where Albertans voted to remain (or not) in Canada

It’s a change of script from 2022 when Smith, then a newly-minted party leader, made waves by suggesting she didn’t need much urban support. Instead, she had mapped out a “rural-based” path to electoral victory, telling a columnist that she’d done the math and would only need a relative handful of city seats if she won everywhere else.
Smith delivered, winning a majority the following year. She took a dozen seats in Calgary and a few on the outskirts of Edmonton, but painted most of the map blue everywhere else.
But Calgary has since rejected most of Smith’s referendum questions and, Young points out, flipped the reliably right-leaning riding of Calgary-Shaw to the NDP in a recent byelection.
“It looks like Calgary is in a different place than it was a couple of years ago,” Young said.

It may not help that Smith, a frequent critic of federal overreach, has waded into municipal issues in recent months, essentially overturning the decisions of city councils on issues like infill housing and zoning, and now appears to have her sights set on bike lanes, Young added.
It “doesn’t really signal wanting to have a relationship of respect with these urban governments,” she said.
“It’s going to be really interesting to watch and see whether there’s a softening of the hostility with Edmonton and Calgary city governments.”

Mayor Jeromy Farkas says he's not surprised most Calgarians rejected the referendum questions, and he will be looking to see how the provincial government prioritizes investment in his city over the next year. (Brendan Coulter/CBC)

But as Farkas points out, a year away from a provincial election, there’s still time for Smith to turn it around. He’s waiting to see what’s in the provincial budget: “I don’t watch what the politicians are saying; I watch what the politicians are doing.”
“We want to see much more substantive investment here locally in Calgary around affordability, public safety and essential infrastructure.”
The idea of Alberta as the land of cowboys and open prairie can clash with its urban reality as, contrary to stereotypes, Alberta is actually one of the country’s most urbanized provinces.

According to Statistics Canada, it had the third smallest proportion of rural residents as of 2021 at roughly 15 per cent. That makes it more urbanized than the national average, and close on the heels of uber-urban provinces like Ontario and British Columbia.

But rural issues play a big role in provincial politics here, Young notes. That’s in part a result of the electoral map, which allows for a smaller number of residents in some rural ridings, in order to ensure remote areas have adequate representation.

Drawing the map to ensure each riding has roughly the same number of people while making sure some don’t become unmanageably large is a longstanding struggle in Alberta. The report from the 2017 electoral boundary commission noted that at the time, the constituency of Lesser Slave Lake had a population of 28,858 people while Calgary-South East had 92,148.
In other words, a vote in Lesser Slave Lake had about three times the punch of a vote in Calgary.

But there’s also the consideration of the economic importance of rural areas, given the extent to which the actual action of key industries like oil and gas take place outside of urban centres, Young said.

History plays a role, too: “There’s a sense, historically, of people in rural communities seeing themselves as the authentic Albertans, the people who are generating value and prosperity for the province,” said Young.

The issues faced by urban and rural communities are actually not that different, but they show up in different ways, said Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative press secretary who is now a managing director at communications and public affairs firm Enterprise Canada.
Whether it’s pressure from immigration or the need for jobs, the real challenge for governments is tailoring the message to respect the different ways each community is affected, he said.
“The policy solutions are going to be different, but the overarching issues are the same.”

Most of the priorities Smith’s government laid out for the new session were likely put in place before the referendum and do represent issues that are important to conservative voters regardless of where they live, Aitchison said.
But he expects to see Smith start speaking to a more general audience as the election approaches.

Under Jason Kenney, the United Conservative Party made inroads in Calgary, and could do so again, argues Colin Aitchison, a former press secretary who is now a managing director at Enterprise Canada. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Aitchison points to the 2019 election as an example of when the United Conservative message was heard loud and clear in the cities. That year, the party under Jason Kenney formed government with the help of most of the seats in Calgary and even a few on the outskirts of Edmonton.
“When [the UCP] made significant gains in Calgary, they focused on jobs, economy, pipelines,” he said. “A very simple message, and issues that resonate for both urban and rural communities.”

In interviews, Smith has pointed out that hers is not the only conservative government to struggle in urban areas. But Aitchison, who was involved with the campaign, said the recent victory of the B.C. Conservatives, in which they picked up seats even in parts of tony downtown Vancouver, shows that the UCP shouldn’t be counted out.
“[B.C. Conservatives] focused on affordability, they focused on pocketbook issues, jobs,” he said. “Those are issues that affect both rural and urban communities.”
For her part, Smith said she’s focused on cracking the urban code, to figuring out which issues are important to voters in Calgary and Edmonton and “prioritizing them in a serious way.”
“That’s what the job of politics is,” she said. “You’ve got to find out what’s bugging people and then you’ve got to focus on solving the problems,” she said. “I’m committed to doing that.”

articles.title: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
articles.summary: The term "associate member" is reportedly off the table as officials discuss deeper economic and defence ties.

blocks.text: For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal.
Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.

The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.

According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement.
The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada.

"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.
Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.
On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.

But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.

Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.

Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

articles.title: Business groups urge Congress to scrap P180-billion infra insertions
articles.summary: Almost 30 business organizations called on Congress to remove congressional additions amounting to almost P180 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 5:49pm
The House of Representatives plenary hall during the first briefing on the proposed 2026 national budget, Monday, Aug. 18, 2025.
Philstar.com / Dominique Nicole Flores

MANILA, Philippines — Almost 30 business organizations called on Congress to remove congressional additions amounting to almost P180 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget in a statement issued Thursday, October 29.

The insertions cover infrastructure projects under various agencies, namely the Department of Public Works and Highways, National Irrigation Administration, Department of Agriculture and Department of Health (DOH).

The business groups, including the Makati Business Club, Management Association of the Philippines and Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry, stressed the importance of a "technical basis," likening the additions' lack of supporting documents to insertions in the 2023 to 2025 budgets that were linked to ghost flood control projects.

"An item should stay only if it is backed by a feasibility study or detailed engineering design, is consistent with the implementing agency’s master plans, and was validated by that agency as ready for implementation in 2027," the coalition said.

According to budget watchdogs, the additions were financed in part by reductions to the respective budgets of foreign-assisted projects, calamity funds, the EDSA Busway and health programs, a move the groups called "indefensible."
Unless Congress can defend each reduction, the group said the funds must be restored to the levels proposed in the National Expenditure Program.
Deliberations on the budget remain underway in the Senate.
The bicameral conference committee, which will reconcile conflicting provisions in the House and Senate versions of the bill, will convene after the Senate concludes its plenary debates.
