articles.title: Shell profits double to $10.8bn as Iran war pushes up profit margin on oil
articles.summary:
Energy firm to return $5bn to shareholders as climate campaigners criticise high profits

Shell has doubled its profits in the last quarter after the Middle East conflict drove up the price…

blocks.text: Shell has doubled its profits in the last quarter after the Middle East conflict drove up the price of oil and gas and created shortages in the global market.

Shell reported on Thursday morning that it made an adjusted profit of $10.8bn (£8.1bn) in the July-September quarter, up from $5.432bn in the third quarter of 2025. The results beat analyst expectations for a rise to $10.33bn.
The company also raised its share buyback programme – it plans to return $5bn to investors for the next three months, up from $3bn in the last quarter.

“Shell’s relentless focus on operational performance enabled very strong results in a quarter with continued severe disruption to the global energy system,” the Shell chief executive, Wael Sawan, said.
Climate campaigners criticised the jump in profits, which pushed Shell’s shares up by 3% in early trading on Thursday morning.

“As fossil-fuelled storms, floods, and soaring costs wreck communities, oil executives like Shell’s Wael Sawan are popping champagne on the deck of a sinking planet. We are paying with our lives and paychecks while they cash in on our misery,” said Philip Evans, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace.
Shell’s profits were also higher than in the second quarter of this year, when it made $9.836bn.

Shell told investors earlier this month that it expected the profit margins at its refineries to climb to $42 for each barrel of fuel produced in the July to September period, far above the margins of $24 a barrel in the second quarter of this year.

These margins are also significantly higher than the previous record for petroleum products of about $28 a barrel, set in the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war, due to shortages in the global market caused by severe damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.

Shell’s gas production has been hard hit by the Middle East crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf. The company’s prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day fell by a third as the Middle East war unfolded.
after newsletter promotion

Europe’s benchmark gas price index reached an average of almost €64 per megawatt-hour in the third quarter, up from more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the global oil price benchmark averaged $94.90 a barrel, up from $69.10 a barrel in the same quarter last year.

The steadily rising commodity prices helped lift the market value of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company, now the largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index. Shell’s share price rose to a record high of more than £40 a share earlier this month as the global oil price climbed towards $117 a barrel, the highest price in six months.

articles.title: More Canadian provinces are ending time changes. What does it mean for your health?
articles.summary: Researchers are raising concerns as parts of Canada move to permanent daylight time, warning that later winter sunrises could have consequences for sleep and health.

image.caption: Clock at Charlottetown City Hall in Charlottetown, P.E.I. As parts of Canada stop changing their clocks twice a year, sleep scientists say the time they choose to keep could have consequences for sleep and health. (Shane Ross/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Researchers are raising concerns as parts of Canada move to permanent daylight time, warning that later winter sunrises could have consequences for sleep and health.
Sleep scientists say ending the switch is good, but permanent daylight is the wrong choice

Millions of Canadians will turn their clocks back one hour this weekend, while millions of others will not. This divide is putting Canadians under different time systems — with potentially different consequences for their health.

Most of British Columbia, as well as Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories are no longer changing their clocks twice a year, joining Yukon and most of Saskatchewan. Most of Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will still turn their clocks back on Nov. 1 for the end of daylight saving time.

For Quebec, this could be the last time. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced Wednesday that his government is moving to end the twice-yearly clock change, but it has not yet decided which time the province will keep. He said that decision will be made after consulting experts.

Research suggests permanent standard time — the time we return to in the fall — is more closely aligned with the body's internal clock than permanent daylight time, which several provinces have chosen.
Here's what winter time would look like across Canada under proposed time-zone changes

Joseph De Koninck, an emeritus professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa, has studied sleep for decades. He said the springtime change is the most problematic because people lose an hour of sleep when they set their clocks forward, creating a mismatch between the body's internal biological clock and solar time.

De Koninck explained that our biological clock uses light to synchronize itself. As daylight changes with the seasons, our circadian rhythms adjust gradually. Making a one-hour adjustment all at once, however, is much more difficult.
"We are able to adapt, but it's not optimal for our health."
The Edmonton skyline at dawn. As one of Canada's northernmost major cities, Edmonton will see winter sunrises as late as 10 a.m. under Alberta's new permanent daylight time. (John Robertson/CBC)
Why morning light matters
Michael Antle, head of the University of Calgary's psychology department and a professor who studies circadian rhythms, said permanent standard time would have been better for Alberta.
Because of the province's northern latitude and position within its time zone, it already has late winter sunrises, Antle said. Permanent daylight time will push them forward another hour.
"It's not the choice I would have made," he said of the province's decision.
Antle said daylight time essentially means society has agreed to get up and go to work or school an hour earlier.
Most people's circadian clocks run slightly slow, making them somewhat "night owlish," he said. Morning light helps speed up that clock.
Michael Antle, a University of Calgary psychology professor, says permanent standard time is healthier because it better aligns with people's body clocks. (Submitted by Michael Antle)
When morning light arrives later, there can be a mismatch between what the body wants to do and what work or school requires.
Antle described this effect as "social jetlag."

Antle pointed to population studies that found people exposed to later sunsets slept less and had higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. He also cited Russian research that found winter depression among young people increased while Russia observed permanent daylight time.
Why some scientists don't support B.C.'s switch to permanent daylight time
Why researchers say permanent daylight time is a bad idea
Both researchers distinguish between the disruption caused by changing the clocks and the effects of living on daylight time year-round.

Antle said the spring change creates a sudden shift that can leave people feeling as though they're living on the wrong time for several weeks. Permanent daylight time would extend that mismatch through the darkest months of the year.
He would prefer permanent standard time. Continuing to spring forward and fall back would be a compromise, he said, preserving later summer evenings without the longer-term winter mismatch.

items: For thousands of workers, lifelong time-zone math will go out the window when B.C. stops changing clocks
Time zones in Canada are getting complicated. These maps lay them out

blocks.text: Night owls who work regular daytime jobs may struggle the most because they already find it difficult to wake up early, Antle said.

Those darker mornings are also having a real-world impact. Ski hills in Alberta's Bow Valley, for example, are delaying their opening times this winter to give staff more daylight to prepare the slopes before skiers arrive.
But most schools and workplaces have less flexibility to change their hours based on when the sun is up.
Changing clocks twice a year a question of public health: prof
Canada becomes a natural experiment
Canada's emerging patchwork could give researchers an opportunity to study neighbouring populations living under different time systems.
Antle said he would have preferred a year's notice to collect baseline data before Alberta made the change.
He said researchers should examine mental health, vehicle and pedestrian collisions, school performance and attendance, and workplace attendance and tardiness.
De Koninck noted that researchers now have tools to document sleep habits over time and compare how people adapt in different provinces.

But he expects Western Canadians may make their feelings known before researchers have years of data to analyze. People may not fully understand what permanent daylight time means, he said, until they've experienced a winter with much later sunrises.
"Those who've tried it haven't liked it," he said.
For De Koninck, the larger concern is what prolonged sleep disruption can mean for people's health.
"If you feel sleep deprived, then you have a host of issues, psychological and physical," he said.
"You can't play with your sleep."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Michael Johnson is a senior writer and editor based in Vancouver. Before joining CBC, he was an award-winning science writer and editor. He holds a PhD in the history of science from the University of British Columbia. He can be reached at eric.johnson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: He tried to get into Montreal's kosher market. It led to a battle over alleged meat monopoly
articles.summary: Mendy Boyarsky alleges the Jewish Community Council of Montreal (JCC) is using its market dominance to limit competition to the kosher meat market through its certifier, Montreal Kosher, known as MK…

image.caption: Mendy Boyarsky sells kosher meat at his retail butcher shop but alleges he is being systematically denied access to some other points of sale. He is asking the federal Competition Tribunal to step in. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)

blocks.text: Mendy Boyarsky is fed up with the cost of kosher meat in Montreal and he’s on a mission to bring prices down.
But the owner of Aleph Meats is facing an uphill battle.
Trying to get a foothold in the marketplace is now leading to a potential legal showdown at the federal Competition Tribunal.

Boyarsky alleges the Jewish Community Council of Montreal (JCC), which operates Montreal Kosher, known as MK Kosher certification, has used its dominant position in the market to squeeze out competition among meat suppliers — like himself — and pressure local congregations to buy only MK approved kosher products.
The JCC oversees many aspects of life in Montreal’s devout Jewish community including the certification of kosher meat through its non-profit MK Kosher. The JCC denies Boyarsky's allegations.
But Boyarsky thinks the certifier is driving up the cost of food.
“They don't allow competition in the market. So they're able to charge exorbitant prices,” he said.

“There hasn't been another option other than the MK in Montreal for who knows how long,” he says, as he proudly shows off the different cuts of certified kosher meat at Aleph Meats, located in the city of Côte Saint-Luc, in Montreal's west end.

Boyarsky alleges his attempts to break into the commercial side of Montreal’s kosher meat industry are being blocked by the JCC and he can't sell to most synagogues or banquet spaces, for example, because they are exclusively dealing with MK Kosher.
He chose to operate outside of MK Kosher’s certification system and to use a different kosher meat certifier — Kashrut Supervision du Rabbinat (KSR).
“We have to be able to sell it to the synagogues, we have to be able to sell anywhere we want to be able to sell to,” he says.
Without access, even if the retail side of his business goes well, he says he won’t be able to scale his business and survive.
“We have to do it on mass production in order for this thing to work," he said. "We’re kosher certified and we need to have all the gates open for us."
If successful, Boyarsky’s lawsuit could force the JCC to pay millions in damages.
A case that could test the new limits of Canada’s Competition Tribunal
Having a case heard at Canada's Competition Tribunal can be difficult, but Boyarsky’s lawyer says the timing may be right to challenge the JCC’s alleged market dominance.

“There's been a groundswell of support from the Montreal Jewish community that wants to see this case brought to the Competition Tribunal,” said Joshua Krane, a competition law specialist and partner at MLT Aikins in Ottawa.

In response to the rising cost of living and skyrocketing grocery bills, Bill C-56 and Bill C-59, were passed by Parliament in December 2023 and June 2024 — overhauling Canada's Competition Act and expanding private access to the Competition Tribunal.
Is there a kosher meat monopoly in Montreal? He’s alleging it's driving up prices
Krane says the tribunal now has the option to consider a case based on public interest grounds.
Federal Court Judge Jocelyne Gagné will decide whether Boyarsky’s lawsuit has merit and will be heard by the tribunal.
In an affidavit, the JCC denies its certifier enforces any exclusivity agreements with the exception of banquet halls.

In those cases, the JCC argues it’s not practical for synagogues to make sure a kitchen is kosher to MK Kosher’s standards every time a different certifier is used. It added that it does not agree with KSR about what constitutes proper kosher standards.
Rabbi Haim Nataf, who was authorized to speak on behalf of the JCC and MK Kosher, told CBC Boyarsky’s lawsuit is founded on “misconceptions” regarding Montreal’s kosher market.

Nataf said it is a mistake for Boyarsky, a meat seller, to claim he’s in competition with a certifier that doesn’t sell kosher products. He denies that MK Kosher has the capacity to influence pricing.
What is kosher and why is it more expensive?
The term kosher translates to "fit to eat,” and what qualifies comes down to standards set by Jewish community leaders and their interpretation of ancient texts and traditions.
“(Keeping kosher) is one of the definitive characteristics of an observant Jewish home,” says Rabbi Reuben Poupko of the Beth Israel Beth Aaron Congregation, who is not taking sides in the dispute.

items: Have a story worth digging into? Reach out to CBC Montreal Investigates

blocks.text: In general, Poupko says the method of slaughtering the animal is more humane and pain free. Every step of the process is carefully monitored with inspections.
But “keeping kosher” comes at a cost.
“I've never heard anyone complain it was too inexpensive,” Poupko says. “It is significantly more expensive than regular meat.”

Rabbi Haim Nataf, spokesperson for the JCC and MK Kosher, says setting kosher standards is a religious issue. He says as a certifier, MK Kosher doesn’t have the ability to set prices. (Karol Dahl/CBC)

Nataf told CBC at MK Kosher, the JCC has full-time employees to ensure its strict religious standards are observed throughout the process. This includes drop-in inspections at restaurants and synagogues and 24/7 video surveillance in their prep spaces and kitchens.
MK Kosher is paid a one-time fee for some services, such as attending a slaughter, and recurring fees for others, like maintaining an MK Kosher certificate for restaurants and synagogues.
Nataf rejected the suggestion that MK Kosher brings in a big profit.
“I wouldn't call it a money maker. It definitely has a surplus that is reallocated to other community needs,” Nataf said.
He calculates the MK Kosher certification system only adds about 51 cents per kilogram to the overall cost of meat at retail.
Montrealers travel to New York to buy cheaper food
But Poupko says many community members think Montreal’s prices are higher than other markets.
“The community is divided between those who are agitated and frustrated and those who have quietly surrendered. But not too many people are happy,” Poupko said.
CBC spoke to several of Boyarsky’s customers who said they travel to New York to buy food ahead of holidays or if they are planning to host a large private event.

CBC’s investigation found that at certain locations in New York — such as Bingo Wholesale, a well-known grocer — there are significant savings on beef. Even after factoring in currency conversion, ground beef was on average 40 per cent to 50 per cent cheaper at Bingo Wholesale than at some of Montreal’s MK Kosher certified butchers and grocery stores.
Frustrated with local prices, kosher meat customers in Montreal told CBC it's common to travel to New York in search of deals. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)
Between Oct. 16 and 19, CBC visited four major grocery chains that had kosher counters and two kosher butcher shops in Montreal to check prices.
Nataf, with the JCC and MK Kosher, says Bingo Wholesale is an outlier in New York.
He doesn’t believe beef prices are higher in Montreal and argues consumers need to shop around.
“I’m convinced there are very reasonable deals out there,” he said.

Boyarsky and the JCC dispute the overall size of the kosher meat market in Montreal. According to documents provided by the JCC as part of its affidavit, Montreal's top three MK-certified kosher meat distributors totaled $37.5 million in gross sales for 2025.
An old practice persists
One of the challenges is there may be a perception that JCC is freezing out competitors because it subscribes to a religious law called Sh’chutei Chutz.

Sh'chutei Chutz is grounded in Jewish law where a community maintains a closed market. Poupko says it's a relic from small villages in Eastern Europe when meat from outside the community was banned to protect local butchers, who played multiple roles in the community such as prayer leaders and mohalim.
While other Jewish communities have dropped the law as a guiding principle, the JCC has held on to what critics now call an outdated standard.
“The fact that there is not significant competition in Montreal is a significant contributing factor to the cost. There's no question,” Poupko says.
But Nataf argues the law is used to make sure traditions and standards are maintained in Montreal.
“I'm not saying it's very popular, but it's still around,” he said.
He argues that the JCC’s interpretation of Sh'chutei Chutz is quite lenient, in part because MK Kosher does certify beef from overseas.
Aleph Meats, owned by Mendy Boyarsky, gets KSR beef from South America, often making it more affordable.
CBC’s investigation found ground beef, for example, was between 18 per cent to 37 per cent cheaper at Aleph Meats than MK Kosher certified products at the locations that were price checked.
Montreal’s Jewish Community divided over the case
Krane, Boyarsky's lawyer, says he’s confident the Competition Tribunal will agree to hear the case. Then the real work will begin.
“We have to show there's been a practice of exclusivity. And then we have to show that that practice has resulted in higher prices or less choice for consumers,” Krane says.
Nataf, the JCC spokesperson, doesn't think the lawsuit should move forward.
Typically issues within the Jewish community are handled internally by the Rabbinical Tribunal of Montreal (Beth Din) — which operates under the JCC — rather than being fought out in court.
“I don't think it's the place of tribunals to interfere in kosher certification and generally religious beliefs and discussions,” said Nataf.
But since the Beth Din is also part of the JCC, Boyarsky says he had no choice but to take this route.
“They’re the prosecutor, they’re the judge and they’re the jury. They get to decide who can sell what, who can bring it in, they control everything across the board,” he said.
Bovarsky added that he's personally putting a lot on the line.
“There's a possibility that I won't be able to go into the synagogue, or I'll be thrown out of the community," he said.
“But if we win … the community will be the major beneficiary.”

articles.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk to conduct his 1st spacewalk
articles.summary: The International Space Station is roughly 400 kilometres above Earth, moving at roughly 7.66 kilometres per second, and today, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be whizzing around…

image.caption: Canadian astronaut Dave Williams is anchored to the foot restraint on Canadarm2 in 2007. Joshua Kutryk will conduct his first spacewalk Thursday outside the International Space Station, where he'll be installing solar arrays. (NASA)

blocks.text: Science

The International Space Station is roughly 400 kilometres above Earth, moving at roughly 7.66 kilometres per second, and today, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be whizzing around Earth while working outside of it to install solar arrays.
This is the 100th spacewalk at the International Space Station and will involve installing solar arrays

The International Space Station is roughly 400 kilometres above Earth, moving at roughly 7.66 kilometres per second, and on Thursday, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be whizzing around Earth while working outside of it.

Kutryk, along with NASA astronaut Anil Menon, will conduct one of two spacewalks where they will install eight solar arrays. After the scheduled second walk on Nov. 5, these new arrays will increase the station's power capacity from 160 kilowatts to 215 kilowatts.
Canada is playing a prominent role in this spacewalk.
CSA astronaut Jenni Gibbons will serve as capcom, or capsule communicator, from the Johnson Space Center in Houston.
She has served as capcom a few times already, including during the Artemis II mission where Canadian Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon with three NASA astronauts.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut and backup Artemis II crew member Jenni Gibbons served as capsule communicator (capcom) during an Orion manual piloting demonstration on the fourth day of the mission. (Bill Stafford/NASA)
Then there's Canadarm2, the robotic arm that was crucial in the construction of the ISS, and which is used to move supplies and catch cargo spacecraft.

It already removed the arrays, called the International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs), from a SpaceX Dragon cargo earlier last week. It later moved them into position on the station's mobile base.

items: Joshua Kutryk's launch to the ISS is another example of the important role Canada plays in space exploration
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he's 'having a blast' on the International Space Station

blocks.text: And finally, the CSA will also be involved at its Robotics Mission Control Centre in Longueuil, Que.

During Thursday's spacewalk, Canadarm2 will help Kutryk and Menon pick up and move each solar array from the mobile base to its final destination. Kutryk won't be riding the arm. Instead it will be Menon.
NASA astronauts perform a spacewalk to install an International Space Station Roll Out Solar Array with the assistance of the Canadarm2 robotic arm in 2022. (NASA)
The whole spacewalk is a demonstration of Canada's capabilities in space, said Mathieu Caron, director of CSA's astronaut office.

"I think what it means for Canada is an acknowledgement of the important role that we've been playing as part of this international collaboration," he said, noting spacewalks and capcom shifts are important roles that wouldn't be assigned to just anybody.
"There would be no way to accomplish this spacewalk without the help of Canadian robotics."
No walk in the park
"It's ridiculously dangerous, but we're well-prepared," said CSA astronaut David Saint-Jaques, who was the last Canadian to conduct a spacewalk in 2019.
"It is a shocking feat of teamwork. But it's an amazing experience to be basically your own little satellite of the Earth."
And he notes that the spacesuit is more than just something you wear.
"A spacesuit is not a piece of clothing. It's not like some, you know, winter suit," he said. "It's a miniature spacecraft in the shape of a human body that you have to fly."
CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk takes part in a spacewalk training session at Johnson Space Center in Houston. (NASA)

There was a close call with European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano during a 2013 spacewalk, when his helmet began filling with water. He was able to return to the safety of the ISS shortly after.
But Kutryk has trained long and hard for this spacewalk, and the crew prepared the suit checks over the past week.
While the hours' long spacewalk will no doubt be daunting, Kutryk will be able to see the world — the universe — as few on Earth have.
"A spacewalk is, for many astronauts, it's the peak of their career," Saint-Jacques said, noting that even thinking about his spacewalk sends shivers down his spine.
He also offered a message to Kutryk: "Josh, I know you're gonna do a good job. You've got this."

Saint-Jacques says Kutryk is a "stellar guy" who knows the procedure by heart, having practised it several times. He says the biggest challenge will be "to take a moment to look around, look at Earth, just let it all sink in."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ontario to provide fiscal update as tariff fight bites into budget
articles.summary: Ontario will provide a key economic update today after repeated warnings from the province’s treasurer that its mini-budget will be awash in red ink.

image.caption: Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy points to the gallery after tabling the provincial budget at Queen’s Park in Toronto on March 26, 2026. He will table a fiscal update Thursday at Queen's Park. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto
Ontario will provide a key economic update today after repeated warnings from the province’s treasurer that its mini-budget will be awash in red ink.
Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy warns budget deficits continue because of trade war
Ontario will provide a key economic update Thursday after repeated warnings from the province’s treasurer that its mini-budget will be awash in red ink.

Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy has been saying for weeks that the ongoing trade war with the United States will contribute to a higher than expected deficit. Despite that, he’s promised to deliver a "focused, disciplined and responsible approach" to spending.
“I don't like deficits,” Bethlenfalvy said this week at Queen’s Park. “But these are the times we're in, and yes, we're going to have deficits for the near-term.”
Ontario closed out the 2025-26 fiscal year with a $13-billion deficit, and Bethlenfalvy has said this year's is projected to be higher. The spring budget forecast a $13.8-billion deficit.
In that spending plan, Bethlenfalvy delayed the province's path to balance, projecting it will be in the black in 2028-29.
He said Ontario has weathered the impacts of American tariffs better than economists had anticipated, but the slower economy is having an impact and leading to deficits as a necessity.
2026 Ontario budget highlights
Province will not layoff workers, Bethlenfalvy says

The finance minister has said the province is putting its ministries and agencies under the microscope to find savings. He said recently that would include “curtailing head counts," but stressed it does not mean the government will be laying off public sector workers.

Bethlenfalvy has been tight-lipped about what the economic update will contain in terms of new spending or policy measures. But on Tuesday, he announced $8 billion in tax relief for businesses in an effort spur investment in the province.

items: Ontario announces $8B tax cut intended to spur business investment

blocks.text: “The world has changed, and so ... we'll be laying out the update on where we're at, making sure that we continue to focus on what's right in front of us and what's potentially down around the corner,” he said.
NDP Leader Marit Stiles is pictured during a debate between Ontario's major party leaders in Toronto on Feb. 17, 2025. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
PCs should cut back cabinet spending, Stiles says
Opposition leaders have criticized government spending, questioning the Ford government’s priorities.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said she’s concerned about the state of the province’s books. She challenged Bethlenfalvy to cut back on spending by cabinet ministers, pointing to an expense scandal that dogged the government this summer.

“He calls himself a prudent fiscal manager, and look at the deficit that we have in this province,” she said. “It's shameful, but look, if they want to talk about tightening belts, they should start with themselves.”

Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser said the Progressive Conservatives have used the trade war as the rationale for many of the policies since 2025, but have offered little relief for regular Ontarians.

items: Ford defends health-care record as hospitals say financial 'crisis' is coming
Ontario to table fall fiscal update next week as province continues to weather U.S. tariff impacts

blocks.text: “What you don't see is a real clear plan for what we're going to do, other than we have tariffs,” he said.

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said the government needs to look at introducing new fiscal policies in the update. That includes a tax targeting the province's wealthiest citizens to help fund affordability measures, he said.

“This is exactly why we need a wealth tax so we can invest in the things the people of Ontario need without increasing taxes on small businesses, doctors, lawyers, like teachers, nurses, everyday folks,” he said. “The super rich in this province should pay their fair share.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Shawn Jeffords is a Provincial Affairs Reporter covering Queen's Park for CBC Toronto. He has previously covered Toronto City Hall for CBC and the Ontario Legislature for The Canadian Press. You can reach him by emailing shawn.jeffords@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
articles.summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.

blocks.text: Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".

Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."

When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".

articles.title: Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches
articles.summary: Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

image.caption: Bayern fans made a banner for Vincent Kompany that read "Get well soon Vincent, we are with you!"Image: Bernd Feil/M.i.S./IMAGO

blocks.text: Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.
"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.
"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

blocks.caption: Vincent Kompany's illness has seen a large amount of support from the coaching communityImage: Markus Ulmer/Ulmer/Teamfoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.
"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.
"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."
Why do coaches push themselves too hard?

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face. It is also telling that Aaron Danks, Kompany's assistant coach, admitted that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge."

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that," coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."
Coaches in need of more support
It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?
"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.
"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.
"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

blocks.caption: Frank Wormuth (left) also had moments where he realized football had taken overImage: Pro Shots/IMAGO

blocks.text: A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.
"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.
"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."
German football identity: Frank Wormuth
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio
Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.
"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.
"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."
Will change come to coaching?

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.
"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.
"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.

articles.title: DENR launches restoration program for wetlands, rivers amid El Niño
articles.summary: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) launched a nationwide program to restore critical wetlands, rivers, and coral reefs to mitigate the impact of drought brought by the strong…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 3:38pm

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) launched a nationwide program to restore critical wetlands, rivers, and coral reefs to mitigate the impact of drought brought by the strong El Niño.

“We are ensuring that our ecosystems remain functional buffers against extreme heat. Protecting our wetlands, rivers, and reefs nationwide is one way of protecting the communities and ensuring environmental survival,” said Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna in a statement.

“By extracting nearly 100 metric tons of waste from Manila Bay tributaries, preserving the delicate hydrology of the Agusan Marsh peatlands, and protecting heat-stressed coral reefs in Masbate and Aurora, we are taking concrete steps to help ecosystems withstand the impacts of El Niño and strengthen the resilience of communities that depend on them,” he added.
The department said that various restoration efforts in various regions have been implemented.

For instance, in the National Capital Region and Central Luzon, the DENR partnered with the Department of Labor and Employment’s TUPAD program in deploying River Rangers to remove 15,267 sacks of solid waste from Pampanga waterways, preventing obstructions and maintaining water flow.

In the Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary in Caraga region, reforesting riparian buffers and monitoring drainage canals were implemented to preserve peatlands that store carbon, regulate water, and cool surrounding areas.
Moreover, the DENR said that regional offices in Bicol and Central Luzon are actively monitoring marine heat stress and coral bleaching in Masbate,Aurora, Bataan, and Zambales.

State weather bureau PAGASA said the upcoming El Niño could last until March or even June. Around 40 provinces are expected to experience lesser rainfall during the dry spell and drought. By January, it is expected the number of affected provinces could double.
Other than the drier weather, temperatures are also expected to rise up to 38.7 degrees Celsius.

The DENR earlier said that it has deployed early warning systems in several regions to monitor the potential effects of a strong El Niño and help authorities respond before severe environmental damage occurs.

The department said the systems use automated weather stations (AWS), satellite-based heat stress monitoring and Geographic Information System (GIS)-based risk modeling to track environmental conditions and identify areas at risk. — LA, GMA News

articles.title: Albanese concedes savings needed as he faces internal Labor pressure on cost-of-living crisis
articles.summary:
Prime minister vows not to slash health and education funding amid political problem over handling of economy

  • Get our

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has ruled out major cuts to health, education and essential services in December’s mid-year budget update, but conceded savings are required as Labor struggles to curb accelerating inflation.

Amid growing pressure from within Labor’s own ranks, as well as from the opposition and business, Albanese said the Coalition was hypocritical in not supporting existing savings proposals, including the government’s plan to reduce the private health insurance rebate for people over 65.

Privately, Labor MPs admit the strong likelihood of the Reserve Bank delivering the year’s fifth interest rate increase next week will compound the government’s political problem over the high cost of living, with some calling for radical moves from the federal government. Ed Husic, the former industry minister, this week said price controls on essential groceries items were needed, calling for caps on the cost of bread, milk, meat and fresh produce.
Australia’s headline inflation rate rose to 4.3% on Wednesday, dramatically increasing expectations of another interest rate rise on Melbourne Cup day.

The cash rate already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years, after four rate hikes in 2026. A move to 4.85% would bring rates to their highest levels in 18 years, putting further pressure on household budgets.
As the Coalition criticises Labor for the rate of government spending, Albanese said he understood frustration in the community and efforts to find savings were under way.
“We will continue to meet over coming weeks as well, as we do consistently, looking for, making sure that appropriate savings are made,” he said, ahead of the budget update due in mid-December.
“What we won’t do is rip tens of billions of dollars out of health and education. That’s what happened last time when the Coalition came into office.
“We’re not looking at cutting funding for hospitals and schools and essential services because we’re a Labor government that understand that people are under pressure.”
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, on Thursday accused the Coalition of being consumed by “weird post-truth stuff” by refusing to acknowledge the global fuel shock as the biggest contributor to inflation.
Transport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran.
Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs were up 5.2%.
after newsletter promotion
“The issue with inflation in our economy right now is really a function of two things. First of all a much quicker–than–anticipated recovery in the private sector,” Chalmers told parliament.
“Secondly, obviously, the escalation in fuel prices that came from the biggest oil shock in the history of the world.”

The government’s plans to wind back the private health insurance rebate for people aged 65 would save about $3bn over four years, money earmarked for aged care services. But the plan appears friendless in parliament, with the Coalition opposed.

Coalition MPs believe they have Labor cornered over the budget and rising interest rates, with the budget update expected to be further buffeted by higher costs for government debts due to conditions in the global bond market.
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said Labor’s budget settings were “forcing Australian families to pay more for everything”.

articles.title: PNP appeals to Bato to 'end manhunt with dignity'
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police called for Sen. Bato dela Rosa's surrender ahead of the week-long deadline.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 3:24pm

The Philippine National Police launches hotline numbers to receive information on Sen. Ronald Dela Rosa’s whereabouts on Oct. 28, 2026, guaranteeing confidentiality for callers and 24/7 access. (Inset) Senator Bato Dela Rosa.
The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine National Police (PNP), on Thursday, October 29, urged Sen. Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa to surrender to avoid "any injuries, violent encounters or deaths" caused by tracking operations.
The statement comes just one day before the end of a week-long deadline set for the fugitive senator to surrender.

Public Information Officer (PIO) chief PCol. Allen Rae Co reaffirmed the agency's commitment to minimizing the public danger posed by the manhunt, clarifying that even the controversial P50 million bounty placed on the senator was specifically for information that would help lead to his arrest.

"It was not stated (in the conditions of the bounty) that you must take him yourself or arrest him yourself," Co said in response to concerns raised by Dela Rosa's camp that the bounty could encourage "armed civilians to take the law into their own hands."
Co also reaffirmed the police's decision to identify the senator as "armed and dangerous."

"He has more than 90 firearms still with him. And as for the 'dangerous' categorization, there is a propensity for him to evade arrest. As can be seen, we have been searching for him for a while now. It has also been a while since the warrant came out. He is evading arrest," Co added.

On Tuesday, October 27, lawyer Israelito Torreon, on Dela Rosa's behalf, petitioned the Supreme Court to reverse its May 2026 decision denying the request for a temporary restraining order (TRO) against the implementation of the International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant.

The senator went into hiding in November 2025 and faces charges of alleged crimes against humanity associated with the Duterte administration's war on drugs. As police chief during former President Rodrigo Duterte's term, Dela Rosa is considered to have helped implement the drug war at the national level.

articles.title: Coroner calls for TGA to review unapproved peptides after death of Australian actor
articles.summary:
Richard Norton, 75, went into cardiac arrest in March 2025 after injecting prescribed but unapproved CJC1295 and ipamorelin

  • Get our

blocks.text: The death of an Australian actor after injecting unapproved peptides could result in tougher restrictions on the substances.
Richard Norton, 75, an experienced film industry fight choreographer, stuntman and martial artist, went into cardiac arrest in March 2025 after injecting a prescribed but unapproved peptide.
Tributes poured in for the beloved actor who worked alongside stars such as Chuck Norris and served as a bodyguard for music legends including David Bowie.
Victorian coroner David Ryan found Norton suffered a cardiac arrest after injecting the unapproved products CJC1295 and ipamorelin, which had been prescribed to him by a doctor.
In findings handed down on Wednesday, Ryan recommended the Therapeutic Goods Administration review the therapeutic benefits and safety risks of the peptides.
That review should consider shifting peptides from schedule 4 prescription-only drugs to schedule 10, allowing them only for clinical trials or other experimental use.
“I am not satisfied that it is appropriate for them to be available to be prescribed by medical practitioners,” the coroner said.

“It is not clear to me how their safe use can be clinically indicated given the acknowledged uncertainties as to their therapeutic benefit and their risks (as yet not fully known) to the safety of patients.”
In March 2025, Norton approached medical practitioner Dr Jerzy Muchnicki, expressing interest in peptide therapy.
The report says the pair discussed in detail what peptide therapy involved, including the “experimental nature of the treatment”.
“They also discussed the potential risks and the lack of other alternative treatment options currently approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration,” the report says.
He had previously been prescribed peptides by another practitioner for fatigue, shoulder pain and loss of muscle mass, the coroner’s report says.
A series of blood tests were conducted to confirm baseline health parameters and assess for any contraindications or underlying conditions that may influence treatment decisions.
Following the tests, Norton signed an informed consent form that outlined the treatment, benefits and risks, including anaphylaxis.
According to the report, Norton was then prescribed CJC1295 and ipamorelin injections on 19 March.
A week later, the actor reported he was “feeling good and the peptide therapy was improving his symptoms”.
Two days later, on 28 March, Norton disclosed to a nurse that he had been administering double the prescribed doses of CJC1295 and ipamorelin.
“The nurse advised Richard that from the following week he ought to only administer the prescribed dose,” the report said.
The report indicates that the doctor prescribed two additional peptides to further improve function and reduce pain.
Just hours later, after injecting CJC1295 and ipamorelin, Norton felt hot and flushed before becoming unresponsive.
He died at the Alfred hospital on 30 March 2025.

Muchnicki was investigated by the Medical Board of Australia, whose independent expert found there was “insufficient evidence that CJC1295 or Ipamorelin is safe, effective or beneficial for human use”.
The expert deemed Muchnicki’s notes “sparse, inadequate and perfunctory and were substantially below the standard reasonably expected”.
The doctor acknowledged the criticisms of his practice, accepted accountability for his actions and expressed sorrow for the impact on Richard and his family, the board said, according to the report.
He also swore off prescribing peptides unless supported by robust clinical evidence.
The board deemed regulatory action was not warranted but forced Muchnicki to undergo one-on-one training for clinical record keeping and management.
The TGA has warned consumers about the risks of importing and using unapproved peptides that are promoted online.
Peptides are often promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, anti-ageing, recovery and performance enhancement.

articles.title: Spain train crash: PM Sanchez calls for investigation as 3 days of mourning begins
articles.summary: Emergency crews worked through the night after a high-speed train collision killed 68 people. PM Pedro Sanchez has pledged a full investigation into Spain's second major train accident this year.

image.caption: A high speed train slammed into the back of a stationary train Image: Javier Soriano/AFP

blocks.text: Spain began three days of national mourning on Thursday in remembrance of the 68 people killed in one of Europe's deadliest train disasters in recent memory.

On Wednesday morning, a high-speed train run by state operator RENFE slammed into the back of a stationary train operated by private Spanish company Iryo in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid.
A British tourist who was rescued from the RENFE train told the Associated Press that "suddenly, everything started falling apart."
"We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over," the man said.

blocks.caption: Workers started to use cranes to move parts of the damaged trains late on WednesdayImage: Oscar Del Pozo/AFP

blocks.text: Emergency crews work through the night
Emergency crews continued searching through the wreckage overnight for survivors and bodies, using cranes to move mangled metal.
Relatives of passengers gathered at nearby facilities seeking information about missing loved ones.
Residents of the nearby town of Urda joined emergency workers in helping survivors, providing first aid supplies, water and blankets.

blocks.caption: Protesters gather outside the Ministry of Transportation to demand accountabilityImage: Ananda Manjón/Europa Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: Teams of Red Cross workers offered support.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia told AFP news agency that many people are in shock and "haven't taken on board what has happened."
"The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.

blocks.caption: Crash survivors wait to board buses outside a municipal centerImage: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to help identify the missing.
Spain's rail network safety in question
Wednesday's crash was Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year and has raised fresh questions about rail safety.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente blamed the crash on an "inexplicable" decision to allow one train to continue after an automatic control system failed along a stretch of track.
He said the RENFE high-speed train had travelled about 25 kilometers before hitting the stationary Iryo train.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who visited the crash site, pledged a full investigation and measures to strengthen rail safety.

"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sanchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."
In January, 46 people died when a high-speed train derailed and collided with another in the southern Andalusia region.
The latest disaster comes just weeks before Spain's November 29 general election.

articles.title: Teodoro urges ASEAN, partner countries to uphold UNCLOS, reject use of force
articles.summary: Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Thursday called on ASEAN member states and partner countries to uphold the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and reject…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 3:12pm

Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Thursday called on ASEAN member states and partner countries to uphold the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and reject threat or use of force.

In his opening remarks at the 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu, Teodoro said functional cooperation among participating countries must be anchored on mutual respect and adherence to international law.

“First, our functional cooperation must remain rooted in mutual respect and adherence to international law, including the United Nations Charter and the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea,” he said.

“ASEAN member states and dialogue partners share the same principles, such as respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the renunciation of the threat or use of force,” he added.

Teodoro personally welcomed, shook hands, and took photos with defense ministers and representatives of other countries when they entered the venue, except China’s defense attache to the Philippines Senior Captain Yang Lei

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision.

In his opening remarks, Teodoro also called for sustaining progress in defense cooperation under the ADMM-Plus framework. He also promoted cooperation in protecting critical underwater infrastructure and strengthening people-to-people ties.
He encouraged the partner counties to focus on strengthening cooperation on food and energy security amid supply chain disruptions and conflicts overseas.
Teodoro also called for the protection of migrant workers and seafarers, particularly those from ASEAN member states and other countries who have been caught in conflict zones.

“The international order must have a special obligation to protect migrant workers and seafarers in recognition of their vital contributions to the global economy and the way of life of the countries wherein they serve,” he said.
The Philippines is hosting the 20th ADMM and the 13th ADMM-Plus on October 28 and 29 in Cebu.
ADMM is ASEAN's highest defense consultative and cooperative mechanism, according to the Department of National Defense (DND).
The ADMM-Plus expands defense cooperation to eight dialogue partners including Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. —AOL, GMA News

articles.summary:
Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau was injured during a drive-by shooting outside Fitzy’s Loganholme in the city’s south on Saturday

  • Get our

blocks.text: A 19-year-old woman who was on a night out with friends has died after a drive-by shooting that left three other people injured.
Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, from Jimboomba, was hit in the head and neck when masked gunmen opened fire into a crowd outside Fitzy’s Loganholme, a pub in Brisbane’s south, on Saturday night.
She died in the Princess Alexandra hospital on Thursday morning.
Three men, aged 27, 37 and 38, were also hospitalised. One is recovering from surgery while the other two have been released.
Police are searching for those responsible for the attack, which happened on a night when the venue was hosting a boxing event.
Det Insp Ian Galpin was visibly emotional as he announced the young woman’s death to the media.
He offered his condolences to Schuster-Togiatau’s family and friends, adding that about 80 police officers were involved in the murder investigation.
“We will not stop until these people are identified and taken into custody,” he said.

“I’d ask our community to reflect on the fact that a 19-year-old woman, in the prime of her life, was simply going out for a night out with friends and has had her life taken from her in the most cowardly way.
“There are people out there who know exactly who was involved in this offence and exactly why this occurred.

Det Insp Galpin said the young victim’s family was “not doing well” and had requested their privacy be respected.

Members of the Judicial and Bar Council panel Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, Rep. Gerville Luistro, with other lawyers and retired justices conduct interviews for the position of chief justice on Oct. 22, 2026.
SC Office of the Spokesperson

MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) has submitted a shortlist of nominees for chief justice and Supreme Court associate justice to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., as the upcoming retirements of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo and Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier draw near.

In a statement on Thursday, October 29, the JBC said five Supreme Court justices were shortlisted for the chief justice position, while 11 individuals were shortlisted for the associate justice position.
Shortlisted for the position of chief justice are five sitting high court magistrates:

items: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen
Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa
Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda
Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao
Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez

blocks.text: Two other senior magistrates, Associate Justices Ramon Paul Hernando and Henri Jean Paul Inting, withdrew their acceptance of their nominations for the chief justice post before the shortlist was submitted.
Meanwhile, the JBC submitted an 11-person shortlist to fill the expected vacancy for the associate justice position:

items: Court of Appeals (CA) Associate Justice Ramon Bato Jr.
Solicitor General Darlene Marie Berberabe
Commission on Audit Chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba
CA Associate Justice Ramon Cruz
CA Associate Justice Maria Elisa Sempio Diy
CA Associate Justice Myra Garcia-Fernandez
CA Presiding Justice Fernanda Lampas Peralta
Commission on Elections Commissioner Ernesto Maceda Jr.
CA Associate Justice Ronaldo Roberto Martin
CA Associate Justice Walter Ong
Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Maria Rowena San Pedro

blocks.text: The JBC announced the applicants for chief justice on October 17 and conducted panel interviews at the high court’s En Banc Session Hall on October 22 and 26.
Screening for the associate justice post began earlier, with candidates interviewed on October 13 and 15 following an October 8 announcement.

articles.title: HPG issues road safety reminders for motorists ahead of Undas 2026
articles.summary: HPG issues road safety reminders for motorists ahead of Undas 2026

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 2:53pm
The Philippine National Police - Highway Patrol Group (HPG) reminded motorists to observe road safety measures as many Filipinos are expected to travel to cemeteries and provinces for Undas 2026.
HPG chief Police Brigadier General Joyce Patrick Sangalang said 761 HPG personnel will be deployed nationwide to help manage traffic, secure highways, and assist motorists during the occasion.
They will be supported by 586 force multipliers.
“This 761 will be playing a major role in decongesting the traffic, safeguarding our highways, and to include our travelers and commuters for this Undas,” Sangalang said.
“This time, all admin personnel of the Highway Patrol Group will be also deployed outside. Dahil full alert po, we have 100% attendance,” he added.
To avoid theft, the HPG advised motorists to park in well-lit and secure areas, lock their vehicle doors and windows, and never leave keys inside their cars or motorcycles.
They were also encouraged to use anti-theft devices such as steering-wheel locks, motorcycle handlebar locks, alarms, and GPS trackers.
Drivers should keep cash, mobile phones, gadgets, and other valuables out of sight and remain alert to suspicious activity.
Before traveling, motorists should check their vehicles' batteries, lights, brakes, tires, engines, and fuel supply to avoid accidents.
They should also ensure they are fit to drive and avoid driving while sleepy, intoxicated, or under the influence of prohibited drugs.
According to Sangalang, a total of 118,600 road crash incidents were reported from January to October 15.
Most of these cases were due to overspeeding with 37,000 incidents. Other top causes of accidents were overtaking, self-accidents, drunk driving, cellphone use while driving, and mechanical factors.
Motorcycles accounted for the largest number of vehicles involved in road crashes with 57,700 incidents.
The HPG recorded a total of 3,816 fatalities due to road crashes during the said period. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Philippine island fights rising seas with nature, not concrete
articles.summary: For years, residents of a flood-prone Philippine island north of Manila have elevated their homes atop layer upon layer of concrete, only to see floodwaters threaten them again.

blocks.text: For years, residents of a flood-prone Philippine island north of Manila have elevated their homes atop layer upon layer of concrete, only to see floodwaters threaten them again.

Burdened by strong storm surges, land subsidence and rising seas exacerbated by climate change, the 3,000 residents of tiny Pamarawan Island have turned to bamboo poles and discarded oyster shells to build a barrier aimed at weakening waves and managing floods.

The unusual approach offers a nature-based alternative for a country still grappling with a multibillion-dollar scandal that drove public fury over substandard — and at times non-existent — concrete flood-control projects.

"We were terrified whenever there were typhoons. We couldn't sleep at night," fisherman Edgar Javier told AFP on a recent visit, recalling how strong waves once brought down one of his home's concrete walls.
"Whenever the waves hit, the wall shakes."
The project began when the city government of Malolos, home to the island, launched a study with a Dutch engineering consultancy.
"(Concrete infrastructure) projects won't suffice," Mayor Christian Natividad told AFP.
While the project, the first of its kind in the country, initially faced resistance from officials and residents working without a blueprint, Natividad said they had "nothing to lose".
"It's like you accept daily flooding or you do something else with risk," he said.
"I chose risk."
Slowing the waves

By May last year, workers, many of them residents, had begun installing bamboo poles packed with brushwood along the coast. They are designed to slow water flow and trap sediment, with the goal of gradually raising the seabed and supporting mangrove growth.
When AFP journalists visited the site, workers were building an oyster-shell breakwater about 100 metres (330 feet) offshore.
Under the searing heat, men in caps pounded wooden stakes used to secure coconut-fibre bags filled with shells on an artificial shore first created with sea sand.

"This breakwater's main purpose is to lessen the impact of the wave before it can reach the community," project manager Lyana Galang told AFP, adding that the oyster-shell barriers work in concert with bamboo sediment traps.
Filipino scientist Antonio Contreras said the Philippines had long relied heavily on concrete dykes and seawalls, many undertaken without adequate study.

"We have altered the environment so much that we tend to work against nature when in fact we should work with it," Contreras told AFP, noting that some design flaws linked to corruption had cost lives.
But nature-based solutions were not a universal answer, he warned, particularly during catastrophic floods, and should complement conventional infrastructure.
Contreras said the approach in Pamarawan could be replicated elsewhere, provided local environmental conditions were carefully taken into account.
Bamboo and oyster shells also need to be sourced sustainably, he warned, as bamboo deteriorates over time and releases carbon as it decomposes.

The nature-based installations, which cover about 14 hectares along Manila Bay, cost 70 million pesos ($1.1 million), including maintenance, compared with around 90 million pesos for a concrete seawall, Mayor Natividad said.
He estimated bamboo will need to be replaced once every five years.
'Our feet are dry'
With its first phase completed in late 2025, the installation has already brought some comfort to residents.
Fisherman Edgar Javier said the breakwaters had softened waves and helped keep floodwaters at bay during typhoons and monsoon rains this year.
"This has made a huge difference for us. We can still feel the waves, but they have significantly weakened. (They're) almost nothing now," he said.
Arsenia Cabigao, 58, said flooding had previously disrupted her livelihood by submerging areas where she dried fish.
"Our feet are dry at last. They weren't before," she told AFP as she sliced small fish in a narrow Pamarawan alley.
The project's long-term effectiveness remains uncertain, with a scientific assessment due next year to determine if mangrove planting can begin, Natividad said.

Its success, he added, would become more tangible over the next decade as accumulated sediment stabilised the seabed and allowed for the growth of mangroves, which would provide another natural barrier.
Vince Dizon, head of the public works department before a recent reassignment, said he hoped the Pamarawan project could be replicated in other flood-prone areas.
"We need to study this, and learn from those who know and have already done this correctly, so we won't waste public funds again," Dizon told reporters on a visit to the island.
For residents who fear being driven from their longtime home, the ultimate test will be whether their houses remain upright when typhoons and monsoon rains strike.
"It's hard to fight water. Now we're trying to live with water," Natividad told AFP.
"We're building with nature." — Agence France-Presse

articles.title: El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
articles.summary: The troops are trying to recover four military personnel who went missing in an ambush on the outskirts of the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince.

blocks.text: El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.

The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.

The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year, the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021.

articles.title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
articles.summary:
Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in…

blocks.text: Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.
The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.

“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.

Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.

“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.

“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

blocks.caption: An alleged scam site in Sihanoukville, shut during a crackdown. The Cambodian authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres.  Photograph: Rebecca Ratcliffe/The Guardian

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.
Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.

The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.

Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.

blocks.caption: Vacated online scam centres in Cambodia. Photograph: Ismail Kaplan/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.

“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.
Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.

With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.

In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.

blocks.caption: Leftover belongings lie scattered in a room inside a closed compound in Takeo province, Cambodia.  Photograph: Roun Ry/Reuters

blocks.text: “Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.

Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.
Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.
The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.
