articles.title: SC seeks Senate, House comments before acting on impeachment vote threshold plea
articles.summary: The High Court instead has ordered the Senate and the House of Representatives to answer their petition first, according to an en banc resolution dated October 14.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 1:34pm

The Senate, sitting as an Impeachment Court, resumes its hearing on Monday, August 3, 2026, on Article I of the case against Vice President Sara Duterte, which concerns the alleged misuse, questionable liquidation and systematic misappropriation of confidential funds.
Senate Social Media Unit / Wendell D. Alinea

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has held off acting on a bid by two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s Senate allies to scrap a Senate rule that lowers the votes needed to convict her by leaving out senators unable to take part in the trial.
The High Court instead has ordered the Senate and the House of Representatives to answer their petition first, according to an en banc resolution dated October 14.

The court gave the respondents a non-extendible five days from receipt of notice to file their comments. The order covers both the main petition and the accompanying request for a temporary restraining order (TRO), a status quo ante order or a writ of preliminary injunction.
The petition was filed by Sens. Robin Padilla and Bong Go.

The Senate impeachment court is named through Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero. The House is named through Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III and its prosecution panel, led by Rep. Jinky Luistro (Batangas, 2nd District).
Because the court required comment without giving due course to the petition, it has yet to decide whether to take up the case at all, or whether to grant any interim relief.
Until it does, the impeachment court's September 23 ruling on counting only the votes from present and actively participating senator-judges remains in force.
In that ruling, the impeachment court held that only senators legally and factually able to take part when judgment is rendered should be counted.

Four senators are effectively left out of the vote with this ruling: Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained while facing plunder charges; Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, who is in hiding amid an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court, and Loren Legarda, who is on extended medical leave.

articles.title: Spain begins mourning period after deadly train crash
articles.summary:
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims

Spain has begun three days of mourning…

blocks.text: Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.

The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.
Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.
The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s rail network after the transport minister reported an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash.
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight to find further victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, according to Agence France-Presse.

Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, told reporters on Wednesday that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.

A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears.

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said “long and hard hours” were in store because “every person will manage it in their own way”. “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated,” Garcia said.
In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.

The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.
The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.

The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People’s party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Israel election results live: count of absentee ballots under way as coalition talks set to begin
articles.summary: With the final count unlikely to shift results significantly, experts say Gadi Eisenkot’s hopes of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu rest on his willingness to work with Palestinian…

blocks.text: Final ballots being tallied with results expected to show no clear winner
Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Israeli election.

With 91% of votes now counted, the current results show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to receive 53 seats, with the grouping of his opponent Gadi Eisenkot on 48 and the Palestinian parties on track to receive a record 19 seats.

The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, and with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israel could be in for weeks of uncertainty, as both sides try to gather enough support to form a government.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet leaders on Thursday for coalition talks. According to the Times of Israel, he will hold talks with Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party.
This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

blocks.caption: Leftwing protesters blocked roads in Tel Aviv on Wednesday evening to demand a joint government of Palestinians and Jewish Israelis. Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, voiced hope that the country could avoid a second election. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” said Herzog, who is tasked with determining which candidate to tap to form a government, urging parties to keep “an open mind”.

items: Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

blocks.text: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition

blocks.caption: Emma Graham-Harrison

blocks.text: Emma Graham-Harrison
Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

blocks.caption: Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, holds his daughter as he casts his vote in Maghar, Israel. Photograph: Rami Shlush/Reuters

blocks.text: Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”
While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.
But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”

Israel’s elections committee has said it began counting absentee ballots at 1am local time. That count is expected to last until Thursday evening, with an estimated 500,000 ballots from military personnel and diplomats to be tallied up.
They are not expected to significantly change the results.

blocks.caption: A voter casts his ballot at a school used as a polling station during Israel’s general election in Tel Aviv. Photograph: David Goldman/AP

blocks.text: Under Israeli electoral law, each voter is assigned a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at. Among those afforded this exception are soldiers stationed at IDF bases, diplomats working abroad, prisoners and prison guards and people in hospital.
These absentee ballots are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted, which is why they arrive in the final count much later.

articles.title: North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles into sea
articles.summary: The latest ballistic missile launch comes amid rising border tensions with South Korea and uncertainty over potential nuclear talks with the US.

image.caption: South Korean television reports on North Korea's latest missile test on October 12, 2026 in SeoulImage: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said.
The missiles were launched at around 12:30 p.m. local time (0330 GMT) from an area near Wonsan on North Korea's eastern coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement.
South Korea's military said it was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness for additional launches while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Japan's Defense Ministry said the missiles had fallen outside the country's Exclusive Economic Zone, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency.
Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, most recently launching several short-range ballistic missiles on October 12.
Thursday's launch comes amid growing tensions between the two Koreas over a border dispute that has further strained relations between Seoul and Pyongyang.
Why are tensions rising between North and South Korea?
Three South Korean soldiers were wounded on September 21 when landmines exploded in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which separates the two countries.
A joint investigation by South Korea and the United Nations concluded earlier this month that North Korea had planted the landmines south of the military demarcation line more than a year ago.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned South Korean demands for an apology as "despicable." She also rejected Seoul's offer of medical equipment.

blocks.caption: Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, has rejected South Korean demands for an apology over a landmine explosion [FILE: August 10, 2022]Image: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last week, North Korea announced plans to resume propaganda broadcasts along the border and deploy new weapons systems in the area.
South Korea subsequently proposed talks to clarify the border and prevent accidental military clashes. Pyongyang has yet to respond.
What about potential US-North Korea nuclear talks?
The rising tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in potential nuclear negotiations.

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met at the demarcation line between North and South Korea during Trump's first term in 2019 [FILE: June 30, 2019]Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: Seoul is a key Washington ally, but Trump's approach has fueled uncertainty over South Korea's role in any future talks with the North.
North Korea's previous missile launch on October 12 came a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim Jong Un this year.

articles.title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
articles.summary:
Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street

Bereaved…

blocks.text: Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.

The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.

They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game released by Activision, which is made up of real news broadcast footage from Getty showing paramedics performing CPR during the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush. Composite: Youtube/Activision

blocks.text: Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”
They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”
The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment.
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.

The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

articles.title: US: Department of Homeland Security data leak exposes details of more than 40,000 employees
articles.summary: The leaked information reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel across several US security agencies. This follows recent data breaches involving the FBI and the…

image.caption: DHS said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public 'when more information is available' [FILE: September 19, 2025]Image: Erin Hooley/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the third major US government data leak in the past month, details on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including officials involved in surveillance, intelligence and undercover operations, were released on Wednesday by a nonprofit leak website.

Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the data was obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" and provided to the group and "journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew."

DHS said in a statement that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it would provide further updates when more information became available.
Transparency group says releasing data justified
The leaked DHS data reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel from:

items: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
Customs and Border Protection (CBP)
US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)
the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
​other DHS agencies

blocks.text: The data transparency group also provided a link to an online search tool that helps the public sift through the data.
Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the leak identifies "key personnel in DHS' ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," according to a statement on their website.
Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and aid journalists as well as facilitate congressional oversight.
According to Reuters, the news agency called three DHS employees based on the data and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details.

DHS said in September that it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities," which are known to limit cooperation with federal authorities — as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration.
The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that the DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months.
Third serious data breach recently
This is the third major US government data breach in recent weeks:

items: Last week, the Defense Department faced a class-action lawsuit over a breach affecting millions of current and former military personnel
In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen data of thousands of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees.

articles.title: Milwaukee Brewers defeat Tampa Bay Rays to become 1st-time World Series champions
articles.summary: The scrappy Milwaukee Brewers captured the franchise's first World Series title, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla., Wednesday.

image.caption: William Contreras of the Milwaukee Brewers reacts after hitting an RBI double in the sixth inning of Game 5 of the World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Brewers won the game 4-1 — to clinch the overall championship on Wednesday night. (Mike Stobe/Getty Images)

blocks.text: MLB·Breaking
The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers playing in the smallest market in the majors are World Series champions for the first time in franchise history.
Milwaukee defeated Tampa 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Hey, Milwaukee: raise a beer and prepare for that parade.

Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings of two-hit ball, rookie Cooper Pratt got two more hits and two RBIs, and the Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on Wednesday night to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.
Members of the Tampa Bay Rays watch during the ninth inning of Game 5 of the World Series, which the team lost to the Brewers. (Kim Klement Neitzel/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Misiorowski left the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee's dugout for the last three games.
The 22-year-old Pratt set a Series rookie record with six straight hits before a sacrifice fly in the sixth inning. Jackson Chourio set a five-game Series record with 11 hits.

The World Series title comes in the 58th season for a franchise that began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee the following year. The Brewers' only previous trip to the World Series in 1982 ended in heartbreak when they blew a 3-1 lead in the sixth inning of Game 7 and lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.
More to come.

articles.title: 'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
articles.summary: A micro-drama will use AI-assisted technology to edit old episodes of the Australian TV soap to focus on Margot Robbie's character.

blocks.text: Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.

Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.

Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.

In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.

"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".

The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.

Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".

Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.

It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

articles.title: Philippines, India pledge deeper defense ties
articles.summary: The Philippines and India pledged on Wednesday to deepen defense cooperation, with Manila moving to post a liaison officer at an Indian Navy-run maritime information center.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 11:11am

The Philippines and India reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral defense cooperation, with maritime security, defense modernization, and military engagements among the key areas discussed during the meeting between Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr. and Indian Minister of Defence Rajnath Singh on the sidelines of the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Department of National Defense

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and India pledged on Wednesday, October 28, to deepen defense cooperation, with Manila moving to post a liaison officer at an Indian Navy-run maritime information center.
Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. made the commitment during talks with Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh in Cebu, where the Philippines is hosting the 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting.
The center, known as the Information Fusion Centre–Indian Ocean Region, tracks shipping and maritime security incidents and shares the data with partner navies.
Teodoro committed to "facilitating the deployment" of a Philippine officer there "to strengthen maritime information-sharing," according to a statement from the Department of National Defense.
Joint defense production
Singh said both sides also discussed the possibility of "joint defense production," among others.

"We reviewed our ongoing defense cooperation and discussed avenues to further strengthen our strategic partnership, particularly focusing on maritime security and joint defense production," he said in a post on X.

The talks built on ties the two countries raised to a strategic partnership in August 2025, during President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s state visit to New Delhi. India became the Philippines' fifth strategic partner.
Marcos said at the time that the partnership opened "a new era of closer, multidimensional, and impactful engagement."
India also invited the Philippines to join the information center during that visit.
Defense ties between both sides have also centered on the BrahMos, a supersonic cruise missile that India builds with Russia.
In January 2022, Manila signed a deal worth about $375 million for three shore-based anti-ship missile batteries for the Philippine Marine Corps.
Deliveries began in April 2024, which led the Philippines to test the missiles in a simulated strike at sea during this year's Balikatan exercises with the United States.
In Cebu, Singh "highlighted the progress" of the BrahMos project under the military's modernization program, according to the DND.
The two navies held their first joint sail in the West Philippine Sea in August 2025, the part of the South China Sea that falls within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone.

China, which claims almost the entire waterway, sent its own patrols during the drills. Its foreign ministry reacted to the patrols and said "no third party is in any position to interfere" in the disputes.
A 2016 arbitral ruling under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) found that Beijing's sweeping claims in the South China Sea had no legal basis. China rejects the decision.
On Wednesday, Singh stressed freedom of navigation and "upholding the principles reflected in" UNCLOS, the DND said.
India has cited the 2016 arbitral award in joint statements with Manila since 2023.
Ship visits, working group vs terrorism
Singh also pointed to reciprocal ship visits, staff talks between the two militaries and the setting up of a joint working group on counterterrorism.
The Indian official cited two exercises held at Subic Bay in late September, including the second ASEAN-India Maritime Exercise, which the two countries co-hosted.
Teodoro, for his part, pushed to expand the Philippine defense attaché's office in India. The DND said this would allow "broader engagement" with India's defense institutions and military services.
He also thanked India for helping Filipinos in the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf.

articles.title: How students toppled Serbia’s strongman – podcast
articles.summary: After two years of protests, a student-led movement has defeated Serbia’s authoritarian leader, Aleksander Vučić, at the ballot box. But can a leaderless movement govern a country? Send your…
articles.byline: Presented by Helen Pidd with Ana Milosavljevic, Milica Jovanović and Tara Blagojević; produced by Tom Glasser, Hanna Adan, Claudia Efemini and Brian McNamara; executive producer Eli Block

blocks.text: Serbia’s political landscape has been upended. On Sunday, record numbers of people went to the polls and voted to end the 12-year rule of Aleksandar Vučić. And who did they back instead? A list of candidates, half of whom have PhDs, put forward by student activists whose protests have rocked the Balkan country for the past two years.

Helen Pidd speaks to the Serbian-American journalist Ana Milosavljevic, the student activist Tara Blagojević and the MP-to-be Milica Jovanović about how the Student List managed to defeat Vučić’s increasingly authoritarian regime.
With victory secured, the hard part begins: how does a leaderless movement choose a prime minister and run a country?

articles.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
articles.summary: A group called the Department of Peace released information on more than 41,000 DHS staff.

blocks.text: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.
A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."
"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.
"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.
The information was put in a database named Icepick.
Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.
Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.
A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.
"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.
Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.
The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.
Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.
Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.

Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.

Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

articles.title: EU countries block Canada's 'associate membership' plan
articles.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wanted to give Canada a special status within the EU. But Germany and other member states have raised objections ahead of a summit in Montreal.

image.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen are seeking closer ties between Canada and the EU [FILE: September 16, 2026]Image: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Union member states have blocked a proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to grant Canada a special status as an "associate member" of the bloc.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other EU leaders pushed to remove the term from a draft declaration ahead of a two-day EU-Canada summit beginning Thursday in Montreal, according to diplomats cited by the dpa and AFP news agencies.
Instead, the revised document calls for a plan to establish "closer ties" between Canada and the EU without membership.

blocks.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at the Chancellery in Berlin in August 2025 [FILE: August 26, 2025]Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: The declaration was approved by EU member states on Wednesday evening and is expected to be published on Friday, at the end of the summit.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa and several EU commissioners are attending the talks.
Why did EU countries oppose Canada's associate membership?
Von der Leyen first proposed making Canada the EU's first "associate member" in September during a speech attended by Carney.
Canada's PM welcomes EU associate membership idea
However, the proposal raised questions among member states because existing EU treaties do not provide for such a status.
Diplomats said several governments were concerned about the lack of clarity surrounding the proposed arrangement and insufficient consultation between the European Commission and EU member states.
Germany, France and Italy were among the countries that raised objections, although they broadly support closer cooperation with Canada.
Another concern was that the term "associate membership" had already been used in discussions about Ukraine's potential accession to the EU.

Merz had previously suggested such a status for Ukraine as an intermediate step toward full membership. Under his proposal, Kyiv could participate in EU summits and ministerial meetings without voting rights.
Von der Leyen, however, used the same term to describe a different arrangement for Canada, a country that does not have a legal path to EU membership.

blocks.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada an "associate member" of the EU during a speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg in September [FILE: September 16, 2026]Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: An earlier draft of the summit declaration would have allowed Canada to participate in consultations on major EU political and regulatory initiatives as an associate member.
It also called for the full scope of the arrangement to be defined by the 2027 EU-Canada summit.
Carney, meanwhile, played down the dispute over the wording of the summit declaration.
He said the precise terminology mattered less than the practical benefits closer cooperation would bring to Canadians.
What will closer EU-Canada cooperation involve?
Despite the disagreement over terminology, both sides intend to significantly deepen their partnership.
The revised declaration focuses on an "Alliance for the Future," a term Carney has frequently used to describe relations between Canada and the EU.
The initiative aims to remove trade barriers, facilitate investment and secure supplies of critical raw materials, medicines and technologies during crises.
As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU
Both sides also want to strengthen cooperation on energy, climate protection, artificial intelligence, security and education.
Canada could gain broader access to EU programs covering research, education and defense.
A new economic council is planned to bring together businesses from both sides of the Atlantic.
The declaration also calls for a study into the feasibility of increasing Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe.
However, EU governments watered down several economic commitments in the original draft.

An explicit goal of deeper financial market integration was removed. Instead of promising preferential treatment in economic security measures, both sides now intend to limit potential negative effects on each other.
How has Donald Trump affected EU-Canada relations?
The push for closer ties comes amid growing uncertainty over relations with the United States under President Donald Trump.
Trade disputes, US tariffs and Trump's territorial claims have raised concerns in both Canada and Europe about Washington's reliability as a partner.
Both sides hope that closer cooperation will help reduce their dependence on other countries and strengthen their ability to pursue common interests.
How could Trump react to Canada-EU association plan?
Trump previously dismissed the idea of Canadian associate membership in the EU as ridiculous.
He also threatened consequences if the arrangement harmed US interests, warning that he could impose high tariffs or halt trade with Europe in several sectors.

articles.title: Europe's youth take to the streets - they feel locked out of a promising future
articles.summary: The last month has seen youth-driven demonstrations across Europe. What connects them?

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
ByKatya Adler
Europe editorReporting fromParis

blocks.caption: Katya Adler

blocks.text: From Milan, to Marseille, to Madrid and in so many other cities across Europe, streets have erupted in colourful, passionate protests in recent weeks. While most started peacefully, a large number ended in shocking scenes of violence and looting. There have been allegations of radical left-wing groups sparking riots intentionally and reports of police heavy-handedness.

We've seen thousands rallying in Rome and Florence. Hundreds of thousands across France. In Madrid, an encampment of tents has occupied a city-centre square since late September. In Lisbon, tens of thousands of mostly young people marched earlier this month. Tear gas and water cannon were used on protesters in Brussels, after young men dressed in black, their faces covered to hide their identities, threw rocks and firecrackers at police. In Albania, demonstrators alleging government corruption are demanding that their Prime Minister Edi Rama – already 13 years in power – stand down.
This continent feels volatile, socially and politically.

I've spent years in Europe reporting from a multitude of demonstrations, both peaceful and violent. I remember well the ardent Catalan pro-independence marches of 2017, the desperation and Molotov cocktails flying through Athens' streets during the 2015 Greek debt crisis, and various outbreaks of violence in France during President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office, sparked by fuel tax and pension reform proposals.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hundreds of thousands have joined protests in France, some of which turned violent

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Abdul Saboor
Hundreds of thousands have joined protests in France, some of which turned violent

But this feels different. Protests are exploding simultaneously across Europe and the majority of demonstrators – both peaceful and violent – are young. Some really young. Among those arrested, there's an eyebrow-raising number of minors. Over half of those detained in Barcelona scuffles last weekend were under 18. Minors were among those apprehended by police in Milan after clashes, according to Italy's LaPresse news agency.

Europe's governments, for the most part, have been careful to distinguish between looters and rioters on the one hand, and loud but peaceful, legally organised demonstrations on the other. The latter tend to focus around a particular cause. In the current protest wave, placards and chants mainly take aim at education grievances, social inequalities and the rising cost of living – though each country also comes with its own unique set of complaints.

What has triggered this public fury in Europe's youth, seemingly so quickly? Are all these demonstrations in some way interwoven? And with major European elections on the horizon, how will governments choose to respond – listening to protesters' concerns, or playing the law and order card to win support from older voters?
Protest 'TikTokisation'
Students have taken to the streets in France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania – a more than 1,000-mile span of the continent.
Demonstrations are often organised in an ad hoc way via TikTok or Instagram. Belgium's interior minister has complained about what he calls the "TikTokisation" of protests.

Student unions play a role in organising marches, but they are also inspired by the actions of peers in other countries, even other continents. Think of the so-called Cockroach student movement in India – a Gen Z social and political protest movement that emerged in May this year, starting with criticism of the Indian education system.

France, where the current wave of student protests kicked off in late September, fuelled by student complaints over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, is a stand-out catalyst in Europe. There's a saying in neighbouring Belgium: whenever it pours in Paris, it at least drizzles in Brussels. The Belgian capital and the town of Liège have also now seen weeks of protesting youngsters.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In Athens, school pupils and teachers have demonstrated over education and the cost of living

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
In Athens, school pupils and teachers have demonstrated over education and the cost of living
In Barcelona this weekend, students were encouraged to demonstrate under the social media hashtag #InstitutsIndignats, echoing the French slogan, Lycées Indignés (Outraged High Schools).

In Athens, 17-year-old Greek school pupil Yiannis Papanikolaou told AFP: "School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained… I think something might change, because of what France is doing, France will spur Greece."
Stagnation and affordability fears

There's a continent-wide sense of economic malaise felt by large numbers of young people – and it goes far beyond education. They worry about the environment, and fret that AI will rob them of job opportunities. They fear the spiralling cost of living could prevent them from finishing their education and stop them buying or renting a home big enough to start a family.

In Madrid and in Lisbon, frustration has focused on the prohibitive price tag attached to housing. Portuguese Instagram-linked campaigns stated "enough is enough" and called on people to take to the streets as peers had done in Spain.

In Lisbon, Carolina ⁠Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher, said she faces losing her home as her rental contract nears expiry. "I'm the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I've done, I still can't make it," she told Reuters.

It's an anger shared by 22-year-old Riccardo, a protester in Italy's financial capital, Milan. "Even if we don't manage to throw the country into chaos like in France or block every road like in Spain, the aim is at least people will start talking about these issues again," he told AFP.

And it's certainly not just young people on the left of politics who are angry. At the presidential campaign launch of French nationalist Marine Le Pen last weekend, young supporters described different concerns to me. Calling themselves the "silent majority" – not (yet) out demonstrating – they say they also worry deeply about "uncontrolled immigration" and safety on France's streets, as well as the cost of living.
Overlapping crises

The outpouring of discontent has spread beyond young people to include trade unions, France's disparate Yellow Jacket movement that protested against the cost of living crisis during Macron's first term, and other citizens' initiatives. This weekend, Kent in coastal southern England saw two protests, one for and one against immigration.
This miscellaneous mix of protests can seem confusing.

Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, speaks of a build-up of cascading, competing crises in Europe, none of which have ever been properly resolved, he says. That sense of pent-up anger is now bubbling over onto the streets.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Anti-government marches have swept through Tirana, the Albanian capital

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Valdrin Xhemaj
Anti-government marches have swept through Tirana, the Albanian capital

"One crisis layers on top of the other," he told me. "The financial crisis of 2007-8, the migrant crisis of 2015, the environmental crisis, Covid, inflation after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and now again with the war in the Gulf."
Leonard says different "tribes" have emerged out of these crises. Social media consumption and algorithms harden their differing perspectives, leading to a real sense of polarisation in Europe.
"We've already seen this in the US," says Leonard. "A sense of 'my crisis is more important than your crisis'."

Nathalie Tocci, a former Italian government adviser who is now a politics professor at Johns Hopkins University, tells me we shouldn't be so taken aback by the protests, or the youth engagement in them.

"We tend to think of youngsters as politically switched off and disinterested. We think they don't bother to go out to vote etc, but they are truly engaged," she told me, "just in a different, more grassroots way. Think of the "Fridays for the Future [environmental movement] across Europe a few years ago, or the demonstrations against Israel's actions in Gaza after 7 October.

She points to the student-led protest movement in Serbia, which recently defeated long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić in parliamentary elections. "It's quite something. They kept going and going, for more than two years. What sticking power will these new European street demos have? That's not yet clear."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Belgian security services say there is "opportunistic" violence on the fringes of legally approved protests

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Yves Herman
Belgian security services say there is "opportunistic" violence on the fringes of legally approved protests
And what about the looting and the violence?
Intelligence services in France and Belgium have described looting on the edges of legally approved protests as mainly opportunistic.

The rioting, they suggest, is a mixture of "mindless violence" – also identified by the Spanish authorities in Barcelona to describe clashes there at the weekend - plus mayhem intentionally orchestrated by youth from ultra-left radical groups.

Tocci reminded me that, in Italy, you can hear the word "maranza" being used by some Italians upset by the perpetrators of destruction seemingly for the sake of it: smashing or burning cars or public bins, for example.

In France, rioters are often described as "casseurs" – people who break things. But in private, some use a more politically charged term – "racaille". Like "maranza" in Italy, it's pejorative slang, generally used to describe disaffected, rowdy urban youths frequently from working-class and/or immigrant backgrounds. It was used in October 2005 by then-French Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, to describe young delinquents and rioters during a tense visit to the housing projects of Paris suburb Argenteuil.

French media has also asked whether there's been an alliance of convenience, however informal or incidental, between two groups of youths: ultra-left activists and young people from France's disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Like the anti-capitalist left, youth from public housing projects on the outskirts of French cities (known as the banlieues) often feel discriminated against, and complain of police heavy handedness towards them.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Puerta del Sol square in Madrid has been occupied by tents since late September

blocks.text: Puerta del Sol square in Madrid has been occupied by tents since late September

The political right and centre in France, including Macron, blame left-wing radical groups and "delinquents" for planning the riots. In contrast to Le Pen's National Rally Party, they have not mentioned a link with past or current immigration to France.

Critics accuse anti-immigration parties in Europe of trying to capitalise from the riots to score political points. In Belgium, the anti-immigration opposition Flemish nationalist party, Vlaams Belang, appeared to blame migrants for violence in Liège and Brussels, describing the riots as "imported" and blaming a failure of integration and of open borders. Belgium's Interior Minister Bernard Quentin has pointed the finger at ultra-left groups.
An ongoing movement?
Fresh mass demonstrations have been planned over the next days in France and in Italy.
Governments are trying to crack down on the violence. There have been thousands of arrests, and Italy and France have promised to impose a "you break it, you pay for it" policy for rioters.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is also making parents of minors liable for damage caused by their kids, including deducting welfare support received by the family. The Civil Code in France already holds parents who live with their children liable for damage they cause.

But some of these European governments may not be in power for long. All the big EU countries have been holding, or will hold, key elections in the coming months. France's presidential vote is considered the most pivotal for Europe. Le Pen is consistently polling far ahead of her rivals. It's assumed the unrest on French streets is helping her, thanks to her party's law and order message.

In Spain, Italy, Germany and Poland, nationalist, tough-on-immigration parties are also polling well. These parties promise to restore order and national pride. Leonard believes populist or non-traditional parties on the left and the right have become "crisis entrepreneurs", using the turbulent situation in Europe to attract disaffected voters.
Meanwhile, Europe's political mainstream faces a crisis of leadership, says Grégoire Roos, director of Europe at the Chatham House think tank.
I would argue they also face a crisis of legitimacy. The fact that so many people - the young and not so young - are out protesting indicates they have failed to get on top of things.

But it's not at all clear that new elections will resolve public frustration. France is so polarised, for example, that if Le Pen were to become president, many predict her opponents would fill French streets in anger.

Modern Europe is built on an assumption that citizens pay taxes and obey laws. In exchange, they get good public services, like education and healthcare, personal safety and a stable society that follows certain rules and regulations.
But this "social contract" has clearly eroded, says Roos.
Looking at the ferment on Europe's streets, this moment of protest looks likely to continue.
Top image credit: Getty.

articles.title: 'I live with a ghost': Japan's haunted homes attract bargain hunters
articles.summary: Properties where someone has died in tragic circumstances can have big reductions in price.

blocks.text: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.
"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.
"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."
While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.
"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.
Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.
Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.
For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."
The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.
But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.
It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.
Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap., external
Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.
